items.title: Three Members Behind Claude Code Leave Anthropic Within 10 Days
items.summary: Anthropic has seen three employees associated with its Claude Code product leave the company within 10 days. The departures include Thariq Shihipar, Anthony Morris and Cat Wu, who worked on the development and product management of the AI coding tool. Wu announced her departure on November 3, saying that October 30 was her last day at Anthropic. Her exit follows announcements by Shihipar and Morris on October 24, when both said they had left the company. The departures are notable given Claude Code’s growing role in Anthropic’s business and its competition with other AI coding tools. In her post on X, Wu recalled joining Anthropic after testing an early version of Claude Code. “Two years ago, when Claude Code was a small internal tool, I asked it to build an RL env. I steered it for tens of hours but never manually wrote a line of code. It worked, I was hooked, and I joined the team,” she wrote. She said the product had changed considerably since its early days, when users manually approved most permission requests and primarily used Claude to answer questions and write tests. “Today, the default is trusting Claude’s judgment to auto-approve. Claude does large migrations and builds new products,” Wu wrote. Wu also oversaw Cowork, Anthropic’s AI tool for tasks beyond software development. She worked with teams across marketing, sales and finance, and helped hire product managers for the company. Wu joined Anthropic in 2024 and was among the people who tested an early version of Claude Code. Anthropic confirmed her departure to Business Insider , which first reported the exit. Shihipar announced his departure on October 24 after spending more than a year working on Claude Code. He did not disclose his next move but said he wanted to take a break before starting something new. “I’ve left Anthropic after more than a year of working on Claude Code and seeing it scale larger than I ever imagined,” he wrote. Morris, meanwhile, announced his departure on October 24. He was responsible for creating Claude Code’s desktop application, which allows developers to work with AI coding agents through a graphical interface. “I created Claude Code on desktop because I believe everyone can be a builder,” Morris wrote. He credited users’ feature requests and bug reports with helping shape the product, adding that their feedback had impacted millions of lives. “Walking away from my best friends, a product I poured my heart into, and the mission was the hardest thing I’ve done in my career,” he wrote. Morris said he would share his next plans soon. The departures come as Claude Code has become an important part of Anthropic’s product portfolio. The company released the coding tool in research preview in February 2025. It allows developers to delegate coding tasks to AI agents, including writing and modifying code, running commands and handling software development workflows. Anthropic said in February that Claude Code had crossed $2.5 billion in annualised revenue run rate. The tool has also helped the company compete with OpenAI’s Codex and other AI coding products. Anthropic is also preparing for a potential public listing. In an amended S-1 filing submitted to the US Securities and Exchange Commission on November 2, the company reported revenue of $16.96 billion for the September quarter, up 47% from the previous quarter.

items.title: I Built a RAG Assistant That Explains Your Electricity Bill — Without Letting the AI Invent Numbers
items.summary: Pakistani electricity bills are hard to read even when you're technical. The total jumps month to month, and the bill itself doesn't really explain why — slabs, categories, rates, and surcharges all blur together. Most people just pay it and move on. I built BijliCheck at a hackathon to attack that confusion directly: a Bill Checker web app with an "Ask about your bill" AI assistant box. You check your bill, then you ask it questions about it in plain English — "why did my bill jump so much?", "how do I avoid this next time?" — and it answers using your actual numbers, not generic advice. How it works There are two halves, and the order matters. First, the Bill Checker. You open the site, fill in your usage, and click "Check my bill." That produces your computed bill numbers: units, category, rate, and total. Nothing about the assistant works without this step, because the assistant's job is to explain these numbers — not to guess at bills in general. Second, the assistant. It uses retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), in three steps: Retrieve. Your question is matched against a small local knowledge base of slab rules and billing facts, using keyword-based matching. This runs instantly in the browser — no API call for this step at all. Augment. The matched facts are combined with your computed bill numbers (units, category, rate, total) into a single prompt. Generate. That prompt goes to a free LLM (Groq), which writes a plain-English answer grounded in what was retrieved and your numbers. The user sees the retrieved reference facts listed first, then the generated answer. That ordering is deliberate: you can see what the answer is based on before you read the answer itself. The design decision that matters most The assistant is not allowed to invent tariff numbers that were not given to it. That's the whole point of the RAG setup here. A plain chatbot asked about electricity bills will happily produce confident-sounding rates that may be wrong — and a wrong number on a bill is worse than no answer at all. By forcing every answer through retrieved facts plus the user's own computed numbers, the system trades fluency for grounding. The answer might be less smooth than a free-form chat, but it can't hallucinate a slab rate. There's a second, quieter lesson in the retrieval step: RAG doesn't have to mean a vector database. For a small, well-understood set of facts — slab rules and billing facts — keyword matching over a local knowledge base is fast, free, and runs entirely in the browser. The fancy version of a technique is not always the right version. Match the retrieval method to the size of your knowledge base. The architecture is deliberately boring The whole thing is HTML and JavaScript — no framework — hosted on Vercel for free, connected directly to the GitHub repository. The one piece that isn't static is a single tiny serverless function in the api/ folder. It exists for one reason: the API key has to stay secret, and a purely static host can't keep a secret. So the browser does the retrieval, and the serverless function makes the one call that needs the key. Total setup cost: $0, on Groq's free tier, in about 15 minutes. If the Ask box ever says "offline mode," it means that serverless endpoint isn't reachable — usually the API key wasn't set or the deployment wasn't redeployed after adding it. That's a deployment detail, but it's the kind of thing that eats an hour at a hackathon if you don't know where to look. Three lessons I'd pass on Ground the model before you prompt it. Retrieval first, generation second. The order is the safety mechanism. Show your sources. Listing the retrieved facts before the answer lets the user judge the answer instead of just trusting it. Keep the demo shippable. A static frontend, one serverless function, and a free-tier model got a working hackathon demo live at zero cost. Complexity can come later, after the idea is proven. BijliCheck started as a hackathon demo, but the pattern generalises: any domain where the model must not invent numbers — bills, tariffs, schedules, policies — benefits from the same shape. Compute the real numbers first, retrieve the real rules, and only then let the model talk. Malik Ali Hassan — .NET & full-stack developer, final-year Software Engineering student. I build Python automation, AI assistants, and web apps.
items.summary_html:
Pakistani electricity bills are hard to read even when you're technical. The total jumps month to month, and the bill itself doesn't really explain why — slabs, categories, rates, and surcharges all blur together. Most people just pay it and move on.

I built BijliCheck at a hackathon to attack that confusion directly: a Bill Checker web app with an "Ask about your bill" AI assistant box. You check your bill, then you ask it questions about it in plain English — "why did my bill jump so much?", "how do I avoid this next time?" — and it answers using your actual numbers, not generic advice.

How it works

There are two halves, and the order matters.

First, the Bill Checker. You open the site, fill in your usage, and click "Check my bill." That produces your computed bill numbers: units, category, rate, and total. Nothing about the assistant works without this step, because the assistant's job is to explain these numbers — not to guess at bills in general.

Second, the assistant. It uses retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), in three steps:

  1. Retrieve. Your question is matched against a small local knowledge base of slab rules and billing facts, using keyword-based matching. This runs instantly in the browser — no API call for this step at all.
  2. Augment. The matched facts are combined with your computed bill numbers (units, category, rate, total) into a single prompt.
  3. Generate. That prompt goes to a free LLM (Groq), which writes a plain-English answer grounded in what was retrieved and your numbers.

The user sees the retrieved reference facts listed first, then the generated answer. That ordering is deliberate: you can see what the answer is based on before you read the answer itself.

The design decision that matters most

The assistant is not allowed to invent tariff numbers that were not given to it. That's the whole point of the RAG setup here. A plain chatbot asked about electricity bills will happily produce confident-sounding rates that may be wrong — and a wrong number on a bill is worse than no answer at all. By forcing every answer through retrieved facts plus the user's own computed numbers, the system trades fluency for grounding. The answer might be less smooth than a free-form chat, but it can't hallucinate a slab rate.

There's a second, quieter lesson in the retrieval step: RAG doesn't have to mean a vector database. For a small, well-understood set of facts — slab rules and billing facts — keyword matching over a local knowledge base is fast, free, and runs entirely in the browser. The fancy version of a technique is not always the right version. Match the retrieval method to the size of your knowledge base.

The architecture is deliberately boring

The whole thing is HTML and JavaScript — no framework — hosted on Vercel for free, connected directly to the GitHub repository. The one piece that isn't static is a single tiny serverless function in the api/ folder. It exists for one reason: the API key has to stay secret, and a purely static host can't keep a secret. So the browser does the retrieval, and the serverless function makes the one call that needs the key.

Total setup cost: $0, on Groq's free tier, in about 15 minutes. If the Ask box ever says "offline mode," it means that serverless endpoint isn't reachable — usually the API key wasn't set or the deployment wasn't redeployed after adding it. That's a deployment detail, but it's the kind of thing that eats an hour at a hackathon if you don't know where to look.

Three lessons I'd pass on
  1. Ground the model before you prompt it. Retrieval first, generation second. The order is the safety mechanism.
  2. Show your sources. Listing the retrieved facts before the answer lets the user judge the answer instead of just trusting it.
  3. Keep the demo shippable. A static frontend, one serverless function, and a free-tier model got a working hackathon demo live at zero cost. Complexity can come later, after the idea is proven.

BijliCheck started as a hackathon demo, but the pattern generalises: any domain where the model must not invent numbers — bills, tariffs, schedules, policies — benefits from the same shape. Compute the real numbers first, retrieve the real rules, and only then let the model talk.

Malik Ali Hassan — .NET & full-stack developer, final-year Software Engineering student. I build Python automation, AI assistants, and web apps.

items.title: These races matter if you care about money, Musk, and the AI boom as Democrats rack up shocking wins
items.summary: Michael Gonzalez/Getty; Brandon Bell/Getty; BI The midterms will be, in part, a referendum on AI and Big Tech backlash. SpaceX CEO Elon Musk bet big on the Texas Senate race. His candidate lost. Democrats also won a key race in Ohio, and retook control of the Senate. The 2026 midterms have arrived, and results are rolling in. Democrats have won control of the House and Senate, scoring a stunning victory in Texas, where Democratic nominee James Talarico is expected to flip a Texas Senate seat in a race that saw SpaceX CEO Elon Musk donate over $150 million to Republican candidate Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton. Beyond control of Congress, Tuesday's election will illustrate the extent of Silicon Valley's political power and the breadth of the AI backlash. In addition to the candidates, there are big ballot questions looming, none more so than the California wealth tax fight. Here's what we're watching. SpaceX CEO Elon Musk Mark Schiefelbein/AP Texas Senate What happened: Democratic Senate nominee James Talarico is expected to flip a Texas Senate seat, The Associated Press projected. Talarico's likely defeat of Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton is a stunning development that some Republicans feared ever since Paxton emerged from a bitter primary and subsequent runoff. Sen. John Cornyn warned that if Paxton beat him, his fellow Republicans would need to spend gigantic sums of money to hold the seat. Enter Elon Musk. The world's richest man has been frequently trashing Talarico on X. More importantly, Musk has donated at least $158 million that has been routed to a pro-Paxton super PAC. The victory means Democrats are now within striking distance of flipping the Senate, a thought that was considered unlikely just months ago. Ohio Senate Sen. Jon Husted, a Republican from Ohio, walks past President Donald Trump Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images What happened: Former Sen. Sherrod Brown is returning to Congress, the Associated Press projected. Brown is expected to prevail over Sen. Jon Husted, a former lieutenant governor, who was trying to hang on to former Vice President JD Vance's Senate seat. Brown, a former three-term senator, criticized Husted for his previous support for data center development. Husted has said the issue should be left to communities and no longer supports offering tax incentives for new data center construction. Earlier this summer, Senate Republicans' campaign arm warned AI labs that if Husted goes down "and data centers get the blame, politicians across the country will take notice — and they will not go near the next one." Pennsylvania 1st District What happened: Bucks County commissioner Bob Harvie is projected to defeat five-term Pennsylvania Republican Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick, per the Associated Press. Harvie focused his first ad of the general election on his call for a data center moratorium. He also blasted Fitzpatrick over the Republican's previous support for a massive Amazon data center in Falls Township, which is in Bucks County. In 2024, Trump narrowly lost the district, but Fitzpatrick still easily won reelection by nearly 13 points. Michigan Democratic US Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed Jeff Kowalsky/ AFP via Getty Images Michigan Senate Candidates: Former Wayne County Health Director Abdul El-Sayed, a Democrat; former Rep. Mike Rogers, a Republican; Douglas P. Marsh, Green Party; Lydia Christensen, Libertarian Party Where it stands: No race compares to the drama of the Michigan Senate race. On Sunday, Rep. Haley Stevens, who lost to El-Sayed after a bitter primary, reversed herself and issued a last-minute endorsement of Rogers. Beyond the headlines, the race offers some interesting policy contrasts. Echoing Sen. Bernie Sanders (and Trump), El-Sayed has called for the government to take equity stakes in AI companies. El-Sayed also wants to force tech giants like Microsoft to divest from AI companies like OpenAI and Anthropic. Rogers, the Republican hopeful, has called for a pause on data center development in the state. If Republicans want to hold the majority, Rogers will almost certainly need to flip the seat. Polls close: Most polls in the state close at 8 p.m. EST. For counties in the Central Time Zone, polls close at 9 p.m EST. The outlook: Cook Political Report rates it as a "Lean Democrat." History: In 2024, Trump won by just over 1 point. At the same time, Sen. Elissa Slotkin narrowly beat Rogers by roughly 202,000 votes. Michigan has not elected a Republican senator since 1994. Michigan 7th District Candidates: Rep. Tom Barrett, a Republican; Sunrise Movement cofounder William Lawrence, a Democrat; Shane Dedrick, Green Party Where it stands: Barrett is seeking reelection in a southern Michigan district centered around Lansing. William Lawrence, a cofounder of the progressive climate-focused organization Sunrise Movement, has tried to tie Barrett to a proposed $1 billion hyperscale data center near Mason, Michigan. Barrett has said that local officials should be able to make decisions about data centers, contrasting his views with Lawrence's support of a data center moratorium. The outlook: Cook Political Report rates it a "Toss-Up." History: In 2024, Trump won the district by just over 1 point, according to The Downballot's estimates. Barrett won by just under 17,000 votes. Ohio 9th District Candidates: Rep. Marcy Kaptur, a Democrat; former Ohio state Rep. Derek Merrin, a Republican Where it stands: Republicans' hopes of defying history and retain their majority run squarely through Rep. Marcy Kaptur, a 22-term Ohio Democrat, and her northwestern Ohio district that stretches from the Indiana border to just west of Cleveland. Kaptur has criticized Merrin for voting in favor of tax incentives for data center development. Merrin has said Kaptur is "lying" about his record, but as part of a sweeping 2017 budget law, Ohio lawmakers voted to extend the deadline for certain data centers to qualify for tax incentives. The outlook: The Cook Political Report rates it as a "Lean Democrat." History: In 2024, Trump won the district by roughly 11 points, according to The Downballot's estimates. Kaptur won by under 2,400 votes. Kaptur is one of 22 Democrats representing districts that Trump also won. Wisconsin 3rd District Candidates: Rep. Derrick Van Orden, a Republican; Rebecca Cooke, a Democrat Where it stands: Van Orden, a two-term Wisconsin Republican, is trying to hold on to his western Wisconsin district, which includes Eau Claire and La Crosse. Cooke, a former political consultant who now works as a waitress, has echoed Sen. Bernie Sanders' call for a federal moratorium on data center development. Cooke has also hammered Van Orden over data centers. In response, Van Orden has accused Cooke of working too closely with tech groups. Polls close: 9 p.m. EST The outlook: The Cook Political Report rates it as "Lean Democrat." History: In 2024, Trump won the district by over 7 points, according to The Downballot's estimates. Van Orden defeated Cooke by roughly 3 points. Google cofounder Sergey Brin speaks with Trump Win McNamee/Getty Images California billionaire tax What's on the ballot: A one-time 5% tax on Californians with over $1 billion in wealth. Two competing proposals would effectively nullify the proposed tax. The sides: The Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West labor union proposed the tax. Rep. Ro Khanna, a Democrat who is a possible 2028 candidate, has lent his support, as has Sen. Bernie Sanders. Gov. Gavin Newsom, another possible 2028 candidate, is opposing the measure. A number of Silicon Valley elites are also in opposition, including Google cofounder Sergey Brin. Polls close: 11 p.m. EST The outlook: There's been little polling this fall. The few public polls have been all over the place. A recent UC Berkeley Institute of Governmental Studies-Los Angeles Times survey found opponents had a 50% to 42% edge among likely voters. Be prepared to wait: California has a lot of votes to count, and historically some races have taken days or even weeks to call. The fact that there are three intertwined ballot initiatives may also make it more difficult for news organizations to project a winner. In the event that multiple initiatives pass, the one that receives the most affirmative votes generally trumps conflicting ones. Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: Georeferencing GenAnywhere Scenes for OpenRoads: A Practical Pipeline
items.summary: The scene arrived in the right town, on the right block, and about four feet below the road. It also looked rotated by a degree or two. Nothing in the file said so. The mesh was beautiful, the textures were sharp, and every check I ran in the viewer came back green because the viewer had no idea what a datum was. What a Generated Scene Actually Is GenAnywhere takes a map selection and returns a textured mesh of buildings, ground and vegetation fused together. It is produced from imagery and inference, not from control points. The export is a scene, not a geospatial dataset. There is no CRS field, no unit field, no list of objects. Treat it like a photograph that happens to have depth. Two Problems, Not One Horizontal placement and vertical placement fail separately. Horizontally, the scene is usually close but not exact; it may use a local tangent plane, or a web projection that is not your project's state plane. Vertically, the difference is bigger. Imagery-derived ground is not a survey, and ellipsoid heights are not orthometric heights. A scene can be a meter low and still look perfectly flat. Units are the quiet third problem. I have seen a scene come in scaled by 3.28 because someone assumed meters, and the only symptom was a road that looked slightly wide. Fix the unit before the control points; otherwise the residuals will look terrible for a reason that has nothing to do with placement. Step 1: Establish the Frame Pick the project CRS before importing anything, and write it down. Convert the scene into that frame, then anchor it with at least four control points spread across the site, not clustered in one corner. I use monuments, bridge corners, or building corners that appear in both the survey and the imagery. Compute residuals. If they disagree by more than a few centimeters in plan, the fit is wrong, and no amount of visual tweaking will fix it. Step 2: Separate Ground From Props The mesh fuses roofs, walls, trees and terrain. For comparison, I extract a ground-only surface and leave the buildings as context. This is manual work, and it is the step people skip. A merged mesh will happily answer a ground query with a roof elevation, and your difference surface will look like a landslide. Step 3: Compare, Don't Design Once the scene is placed, I build a difference surface against the surveyed terrain. Mean and maximum deviation tell me whether the scene is usable as context. On this corridor, the mean was 0.2 meters and the maximum was 1.8 at a tree line. That is fine for a visual and useless for a vertical curve. The Import Pattern In OpenRoads, the scene comes in as a reference, never as design geometry. I attach it to a layer named for the source and date, scale it correctly, and freeze it. items.summary_html:
The scene arrived in the right town, on the right block, and about four feet below the road. It also looked rotated by a degree or two. Nothing in the file said so. The mesh was beautiful, the textures were sharp, and every check I ran in the viewer came back green because the viewer had no idea what a datum was.

What a Generated Scene Actually Is

GenAnywhere takes a map selection and returns a textured mesh of buildings, ground and vegetation fused together. It is produced from imagery and inference, not from control points. The export is a scene, not a geospatial dataset. There is no CRS field, no unit field, no list of objects. Treat it like a photograph that happens to have depth.

Two Problems, Not One

Horizontal placement and vertical placement fail separately. Horizontally, the scene is usually close but not exact; it may use a local tangent plane, or a web projection that is not your project's state plane. Vertically, the difference is bigger. Imagery-derived ground is not a survey, and ellipsoid heights are not orthometric heights. A scene can be a meter low and still look perfectly flat.
Units are the quiet third problem. I have seen a scene come in scaled by 3.28 because someone assumed meters, and the only symptom was a road that looked slightly wide. Fix the unit before the control points; otherwise the residuals will look terrible for a reason that has nothing to do with placement.

Step 1: Establish the Frame

Pick the project CRS before importing anything, and write it down. Convert the scene into that frame, then anchor it with at least four control points spread across the site, not clustered in one corner. I use monuments, bridge corners, or building corners that appear in both the survey and the imagery. Compute residuals. If they disagree by more than a few centimeters in plan, the fit is wrong, and no amount of visual tweaking will fix it.

Step 2: Separate Ground From Props

The mesh fuses roofs, walls, trees and terrain. For comparison, I extract a ground-only surface and leave the buildings as context. This is manual work, and it is the step people skip. A merged mesh will happily answer a ground query with a roof elevation, and your difference surface will look like a landslide.

Step 3: Compare, Don't Design

Once the scene is placed, I build a difference surface against the surveyed terrain. Mean and maximum deviation tell me whether the scene is usable as context. On this corridor, the mean was 0.2 meters and the maximum was 1.8 at a tree line. That is fine for a visual and useless for a vertical curve.

The Import Pattern

In OpenRoads, the scene comes in as a reference, never as design geometry. I attach it to a layer named for the source and date, scale it correctly, and freeze it. The terrain surface, the alignment, the corridor and the drainage stay native. iTwin handles review; ProjectWise handles revisions. The reference is replaced when a newer scene is generated, and the design does not move.

What Doesn't Transfer

A corridor is not a mesh. OpenRoads carries templates, superelevation, stationing, utility crossings and rules. The scene carries pixels and triangles. There is no automatic conversion in either direction, and the attempts I have seen produce a model that looks right and cannot answer a single design question. The import is manual for a reason: it forces you to decide what the scene is allowed to influence. Decimation helps here. I cap the reference at a few hundred thousand triangles so the design file stays usable on a normal machine.

The Checklist I Run

Project CRS set and recorded. Scene converted and anchored to four or more control points. Residuals under five centimeters. Ground extracted. Difference surface checked. Scene attached as a frozen reference. Source date and imagery date written into the layer name. Every one of these takes minutes and saves days.

The Honest Summary

A generated scene is excellent at answering what a place looks like. OpenRoads is the tool that answers where the road goes, how it drains, and what it costs. The seam between them is a coordinate system and a layer name. Get those two right, and the rest of the pipeline behaves.

items.title: La molécule qui a survécu à 115 millions d'années — et pourquoi j'ai passé deux ans à construire un casque VR pour la regarder…
items.summary: La molécule qui a survécu à 115 millions d'années — et pourquoi j'ai passé deux ans à construire un casque VR pour la regarder de l'intérieur Quand j'ai vu passer la nouvelle, je me suis figé au milieu de ma cuisine, une tasse de café à moitié froide dans la main gauche. Des chercheurs venaient d'extraire une molécule organique intacte — préservée pendant environ 115 millions d'années, coincée dans une matrice minérale que le temps avait fini par sceller comme une capsule. Le genre de découverte qui fait lever les sourcils même quand on n'est pas chimiste. Moi, je suis développeur. Je passe mes journées à faire tenir des systèmes dans des conteneurs et mes nuits à me demander pourquoi mes shaders plantent au démarrage. Mais cette histoire m'a attrapé quelque part entre la gorge et la poitrine. Une molécule qui traverse cent quinze millions d'années, ça veut dire qu'elle était là bien avant nous, bien avant les dinosaures qu'on connaît, bien avant que la notion même de « nous » ait un sens. Et pourtant, on ne peut la voir qu'à travers un écran. Une image. Une capture. Une projection plate de quelque chose qui, à l'échelle humaine, n'a ni haut ni bas ni gauche ni droite. C'est ce décalage qui m'a obsédé. Le problème n'est pas la donnée. C'est la caméra. Dans mon métier, on répète souvent que les données ne mentent pas. C'est faux. Les données sont fidèles à la manière dont on les capture. Une molécule, c'est un objet en trois dimensions avec des angles de liaison, des torsions, des distances interatomiques qui varient selon l'environnement. Quand on la représente sur une page web, on choisit une projection. On choisit un point de vue. On choisit, en quelque sorte, ce que le spectateur ne verra jamais. J'ai commencé par un petit projet perso : un visualiseur de structures moléculaires dans le navigateur. Rien de fou. Un canvas, des coordonnées, une rotation lente. Sauf que très vite, j'ai buté sur un mur classique : le rendu 2D d'un objet 3D dépend d'une convention de projection, et cette convention efface de l'information. Pour la plupart des usages scientifiques, ce n'est pas grave. Pour ce que je voulais montrer — l'impression d'être à l'intérieur de la structure, pas devant — c'était rédhibitoire. Alors j'ai basculé sur un casque VR. Deux ans, trois erreurs, et une décision d'architecture Je ne vais pas prétendre que c'était linéaire. Ça a été deux ans de tâtonnements, avec des moments où je me demandais sérieusement pourquoi je ne faisais pas juste un site web comme tout le monde. Ma première erreur a été de croire que le plus dur serait le rendu. Faux. Le plus dur, c'est la cohérence entre la scène et le regard. En VR, si la profondeur perçue ne correspond pas à la géométrie réelle, le cerveau décroche en quelques secondes. Nausée, vertige, abandon. J'ai passé des semaines à calibrer des distances interatomiques pour qu'elles restent crédibles à l'échelle du casque, sans trahir la structure scientifique. Ma deuxième erreur : avoir voulu tout charger d'un coup. Une molécule, ce n'est pas juste quelques points. C'est un graphe, avec des liaisons, des atomes, parfois des milliers de coordonnées. Mon premier prototype chargeait tout en mémoire et rendait tout à chaque frame. Résultat : un framerate qui s'effondrait dès que la structure grossissait. J'ai fini par adopter une approche par niveaux de détail — ce qu'on appelle communément LOD (level of detail) — en ne rendant les atomes lointains que sous forme de sphères simplifiées, et en réservant la géométrie fine à ce qui est proche du regard. Ma troisième erreur, plus insidieuse : avoir cru que l'immersion se jouerait au niveau graphique. En réalité, elle se joue au niveau du mouvement . C'est la parallaxe, la manière dont les objets proches glissent plus vite que les objets lointains quand on tourne la tête, qui donne la sensation d'être dedans. J'ai réécrit mon pipeline de rendu trois fois avant de comprendre ça. Ce que ça change, concrètement Quand la molécule de 115 millions d'années apparaît devant vous dans le casque, elle n'est plus une illustration. Elle a une présence. On peut tourner autour. On peut s'approcher d'un groupe fonctionnel et voir comment il se tortille. On peut reculer et prendre la mesure de l'ensemble. Et surtout — c'est ce qui m'a le plus surpris — on peut rester . Rester à regarder quelque chose qui a traversé un temps qu'aucun cerveau humain ne peut vraiment se représenter. Pour un développeur, la leçon technique est simple : la 3D ne se résume pas à un pipeline de rendu. C'est un pipeline de perception. Chaque choix — projection, LOD, parallaxe, latence — façonne ce que l'utilisateur croit voir. Si vous construisez de la visualisation, vous ne construisez pas des images. Vous construisez des conditions de compréhension. Pour le reste d'entre nous, la leçon est plus douce. Certaines choses méritent qu'on les regarde autrement qu'à plat. Une molécule vieille de 115 millions d'années en fait partie. Un souvenir aussi, parfois. Une idée qui traîne depuis trop longtemps dans un coin de la tête, et qu'on n'a jamais pris le temps de regarder en face. Un pont honnête Je ne prétends pas avoir résolu un problème scientifique. Je n'ai pas de publication, pas de laboratoire, pas de financement. J'ai construit un casque VR pour regarder des structures moléculaires de l'intérieur, et ça m'a appris plus sur la perception que dix ans de lecture de docs. Si vous êtes développeur, curieux, ou juste quelqu'un qui a envie de voir une molécule autrement qu'en capture d'écran, le projet vit ici : https://sciencereader.com Pas de promesse magique. Juste une porte. Et derrière, quelque chose qui attend depuis très, très longtemps.

items.title: How to Build a Super-Agent Like DeepSeek's: Router, Workers and Triggers Explained
items.summary: To build a super-agent like the one DeepSeek Harness describes, split your agent into two layers: one long-lived Router session that talks to humans and dispatches work, and many isolated Worker sessions that each run one task with full tools. Feed both from event Triggers (chat, GitHub, CI), route follow-ups by Thread , and add a separate Watchdog that checks on everything. Try Apidog today This guide turns DeepSeek Harness's design essay, "Exploring Super-agent Design" , into a build order. One caveat: the essay describes architecture, not a shipped feature. Parts of it live in a prototype plugin called dsh-superagent-prototype , which the authors say is "not an official DeepSeek product." Every code sketch below is illustrative, not DeepSeek's code. What is a super-agent? A super-agent is a single, always-online AI teammate that receives events from many channels (chat, pull requests, CI), runs many tasks in parallel in isolated sessions, and replies to people as one consistent identity. The problem: agent sessions are isolated, and "a person can usually follow only 3 to 5 active sessions at once." A single task is limited by the model. Multi-tasking is limited by human attention. The super-agent targets the second limit. It has four traits: Continuous: one agent across IM and GitHub. You discuss Plan A in chat, switch to Plan B in a PR comment, and it follows. Productive: it runs tasks in parallel and takes your next instruction before the last one finishes. Proactive: it watches events and stays quiet unless something needs it. Persistent: it's always online and recovers on its own. If you're new to the harness itself, start with what DeepSeek Harness is and how it compares with Claude Code . Super-agent architecture: the five modules The essay has five modules. Here they are with the step where you'd build each: Module What it does Build step Two-level architecture Router dispatches, Workers execute 1 Event-driven Triggers Turn chat, GitHub and CI events into agent input 2 Full-duplex, multi-channel Async tools, channel-aware replies 4 Compute, state, environment split Stateless loop, state in a DB, machines stay put 5 Watchdog Separate session that checks progress and errors 6 Step 1: Split the Router from the Workers The Router is one long-lived session. It handles all human interaction and all dispatch, and it never executes tasks itself. It can run without a Bash tool, and a lighter, cheaper model is enough. When several Triggers arrive during one Router turn, they're batched into the next call: long input, short output, merged in prefill. Each Worker is one isolated session per task. It gets full tools and the strongest model you can afford. It never talks to humans; it reports back to the Router. A Worker can itself use subagents, or be a whole agent team. Don't confuse this with an agent team. A team lead decomposes one coupled task; the Router only dispatches independent tasks. You can stack them. # Illustrative sketch, not DeepSeek's code class Router : def on_events ( self , batch ): # triggers arriving mid-turn are batched plan = self . llm_light . decide ( batch ) # dispatch, reply, or ignore for task in plan . new_tasks : Worker . spawn ( task , model = " strongest " , tools = " all " , report_to = self ) for msg in plan . replies : self . channels . send ( msg ) # only the Router speaks to humans Step 2: Turn events into Triggers Every input to a super-agent is a Trigger: a chat message, a GitHub webhook event , a Slack Events API payload or a CI callback. Most of them shouldn't reach a model at all, so the essay filters in two passes. Fast path, in code. Filter by source, group, and user or bot allowlists. Each source gets a mode: "respond only to explicit requests," "candidate," or "ignore." Slow path, with an LLM. Candidates go to a model that applies policies written as prompts, such as "reply when someone reports a bug in this channel." Your intake endpoint should acknowledge fast and work later. GitHub's webhook best practices ask you to respond with a 2XX within 10 seconds, which a model call can't promise. Return 202 Accepted , queue the Trigger, and let the Router pick it up. Our guide to designing reliable webhooks covers retries and idempotency for this layer. Step 3: Route follow-ups by Thread A Thread is a run of consecutive events on one PR, one IM topic or one email chain. The Worker created for a Thread's first event subscribes to it. Follow-up events then pass straight to that Worker, with no Router call. The mapping is many-to-many. If two Workers touch the same PR, both receive its events, and they can resolve conflicts through the PR itself without messaging each other directly. Skip this step and you pay: in the essay's experiment, removing pass-through made the Router take about 30% more decisions and raised token use by about 37%. Step 4: Treat context as a cache and make tools async The Router can't hold everything, so the essay treats context like a cache: Inline what's likely needed: IDs, short summaries, neighboring messages. Spill the rest: truncate it and leave a pointer the agent can follow. Stable IDs on Triggers, Threads and Workers form a reference graph the authors call a "Chain of Recall." The agent hops from a Trigger to its Thread to the Worker that handled it, which gives it multi-hop recall without a giant prompt. Then go full-duplex . Replace a blocking run() tool with async start() and stop() . start() returns "Started" right away, and the result arrives later as a new event. That's what lets the agent take your next instruction while the last one is still running. The essay says DeepSeek Harness implements this but doesn't enable it by default. Finally, make replies channel-aware . Their tested rule caps IM replies at 100 words, while GitHub, email and docs get structured, dense write-ups. It also enables speculative execution : in their user group, a "silently reproduce and fix" policy delivers only a confirmed simple fix and otherwise stays quiet. Step 5: Separate compute, state and environments Run the agent loop in stateless cloud containers and keep session state in a database. Environments stay where they are: each machine runs a lightweight daemon, which the essay calls BYOM (Bring Your Own Machine). A crashed loop restarts anywhere and reloads its state, while repos stay on their machines. The essay points to Anthropic's "Scaling Managed Agents: Decoupling the brain from the hands" as the same idea, aimed at managed sandboxes rather than your own machines. Step 6: Add a Watchdog The Watchdog is a separate session on a schedule, outside the main system. It handles API errors and asks a model whether each Worker is making progress or drifting. Maintainers can also ask it directly why something failed. Keep it outside the Router's process so a stuck Router can't take its monitor down. What the experiments showed The authors ran about 300 chat and CI messages containing about 20 work requests, simulated the coding with a timer, and ran each setup 5 times. They call the results "indicative only." Setup p50 (min) p95 (min) Cache-read tokens per run Super-agent 12.4 15.7 23.2M Without Thread pass-through 12.6 15.5 31.8M Single session + subagent tool, neutral prompt 20.4 29.5 6.1M Single session, delegation-first prompt 13.8 29.0 10.8M Two findings stand out. With a neutral prompt, the single session never delegated in 5 runs, so its p95 was nearly double the super-agent's. A delegation-first prompt fixed the median but not the tail. The super-agent costs more tokens than a single session, so you're trading tokens for latency and attention. A second test loaded the Router alone. As Triggers rose from 1 to 40 per minute, batch size grew from 1.0 to 2.8 and time per request went from 2.5 s to 3.9 s, while time per decision fell from 6.4 s to 1.6 s. Batching is what keeps a single Router from becoming the bottleneck early. Test your Trigger intake with Apidog CLI Every Trigger starts life as an HTTP request hitting your intake endpoint, so that endpoint is the first thing worth testing. If it drops a PR comment or assigns a new thread_id to each event, Thread routing breaks and every follow-up goes back through the Router. Let your coding agent write and run that test with Apidog CLI . npm install -g apidog-cli@latest apidog auth login --with-token npx -y skills add https://apidog.com # pick your agent when prompted Then give your agent one [REDACTED PROMPT] In Apidog project , create POST /triggers/github for a GitHub pull_request_review_comment webhook. Add a test case that sends two comments on the same PR and asserts: status 202, a trigger_id in the body, and the same thread_id both times. Run it against staging and summarize any failures. The agent reads each payload schema, validates its JSON, writes the endpoint and the case, and runs it: bash apidog cli-schema get endpoint-create apidog cli-schema validate endpoint-create --file endpoint.json apidog endpoint create --project --file endpoint.json apidog cli-schema get test-case-create apidog cli-schema validate test-case-create --file case.json apidog test-case create --project --file case.json apidog run --test-case --project -e -r cli,json The same `apidog run` call with `-r junit` drops into your pipeline; see [Apidog CLI in CI/CD](http://apidog.com/blog/apidog-cli-ci-cd-pipeline?utm_source=dev.to&utm_medium=wanda&utm_content=n8n-post-automation). If your agent is DeepSeek Harness itself, follow [this setup guide](http://apidog.com/blog/apidog-cli-in-deepseek-harness?utm_source=dev.to&utm_medium=wanda&utm_content=n8n-post-automation); for Claude Code, use [this one](http://apidog.com/blog/apidog-cli-in-claude-code?utm_source=dev.to&utm_medium=wanda&utm_content=n8n-post-automation). Apidog's Free plan covers up to 4 users. ## Open problems The essay lists what isn't solved: - **Scaling the Router** and choosing a Worker topology as load grows. - **Long-term memory** beyond the Chain of Recall. - **UX without sessions:** steering an agent with no single chat window. - **Context boundaries and agent-to-agent protocols**, where [A2A](http://apidog.com/blog/what-is-agent2agent-a2a?utm_source=dev.to&utm_medium=wanda&utm_content=n8n-post-automation) is one candidate. - **Security.** A prompt injection that reaches the cloud loop could reach every connected machine, and credentials in context can leak. The authors want agents to use credentials without ever seeing them. ## FAQ **Is the super-agent a DeepSeek Harness feature I can turn on?** No. The essay describes architecture. Parts exist in the `dsh-superagent-prototype` plugin, which the authors say is not an official DeepSeek product. Full-duplex tools are implemented but off by default. **Why does the Router use a lighter model?** It only dispatches and talks to people; it never executes tasks or needs Bash. Workers do the heavy reasoning with the strongest model. **How is a super-agent different from an agent team?** A team lead splits one coupled task into parts. The Router dispatches independent tasks. A Worker can run its own agent team inside the super-agent. **What is Thread pass-through?** Follow-up events on a PR, IM topic or email chain go straight to the Worker that owns that Thread, skipping the Router. Removing it raised token use by about 37% in their test. **Does a super-agent save tokens?** Not against a single session. It used 23.2M cache-read tokens per run versus 6.1M to 10.8M, in exchange for a p95 of 15.7 minutes instead of about 29.

Feed both from event Triggers (chat, GitHub, CI), route follow-ups by Thread, and add a separate Watchdog that checks on everything.

This guide turns DeepSeek Harness's design essay, "Exploring Super-agent Design", into a build order. One caveat: the essay describes architecture, not a shipped feature. Parts of it live in a prototype plugin called dsh-superagent-prototype, which the authors say is "not an official DeepSeek product." Every code sketch below is illustrative, not DeepSeek's code.

What is a super-agent?

A super-agent is a single, always-online AI teammate that receives events from many channels (chat, pull requests, CI), runs many tasks in parallel in isolated sessions, and replies to people as one consistent identity.

The problem: agent sessions are isolated, and "a person can usually follow only 3 to 5 active sessions at once." A single task is limited by the model. Multi-tasking is limited by human attention. The super-agent targets the second limit.

It has four traits:

  • Continuous: one agent across IM and GitHub. You discuss Plan A in chat, switch to Plan B in a PR comment, and it follows.
  • Productive: it runs tasks in parallel and takes your next instruction before the last one finishes.
  • Proactive: it watches events and stays quiet unless something needs it.
  • Persistent: it's always online and recovers on its own.

If you're new to the harness itself, start with what DeepSeek Harness is and how it compares with Claude Code.

Super-agent architecture: the five modules

The essay has five modules. Here they are with the step where you'd build each:

Module What it does Build step Two-level architecture Router dispatches, Workers execute 1 Event-driven Triggers Turn chat, GitHub and CI events into agent input 2 Full-duplex, multi-channel Async tools, channel-aware replies 4 Compute, state, environment split Stateless loop, state in a DB, machines stay put 5 Watchdog Separate session that checks progress and errors 6

Step 1: Split the Router from the Workers

The Router is one long-lived session. It handles all human interaction and all dispatch, and it never executes tasks itself. It can run without a Bash tool, and a lighter, cheaper model is enough. When several Triggers arrive during one Router turn, they're batched into the next call: long input, short output, merged in prefill.

Each Worker is one isolated session per task. It gets full tools and the strongest model you can afford. It never talks to humans; it reports back to the Router. A Worker can itself use subagents, or be a whole agent team.

Don't confuse this with an agent team. A team lead decomposes one coupled task; the Router only dispatches independent tasks. You can stack them.

# Illustrative sketch, not DeepSeek's code
class Router:
    def on_events(self, batch):              # triggers arriving mid-turn are batched
        plan = self.llm_light.decide(batch)  # dispatch, reply, or ignore
        for task in plan.new_tasks:
            Worker.spawn(task, model="strongest", tools="all", report_to=self)
        for msg in plan.replies:
            self.channels.send(msg)          # only the Router speaks to humans
Step 2: Turn events into Triggers

Every input to a super-agent is a Trigger: a chat message, a GitHub webhook event, a Slack Events API payload or a CI callback. Most of them shouldn't reach a model at all, so the essay filters in two passes.

  1. Fast path, in code. Filter by source, group, and user or bot allowlists. Each source gets a mode: "respond only to explicit requests," "candidate," or "ignore."
  2. Slow path, with an LLM. Candidates go to a model that applies policies written as prompts, such as "reply when someone reports a bug in this channel."

Your intake endpoint should acknowledge fast and work later. GitHub's webhook best practices ask you to respond with a 2XX within 10 seconds, which a model call can't promise. Return 202 Accepted, queue the Trigger, and let the Router pick it up. Our guide to designing reliable webhooks covers retries and idempotency for this layer.

Step 3: Route follow-ups by Thread

A Thread is a run of consecutive events on one PR, one IM topic or one email chain. The Worker created for a Thread's first event subscribes to it. Follow-up events then pass straight to that Worker, with no Router call.

The mapping is many-to-many. If two Workers touch the same PR, both receive its events, and they can resolve conflicts through the PR itself without messaging each other directly.

Skip this step and you pay: in the essay's experiment, removing pass-through made the Router take about 30% more decisions and raised token use by about 37%.

Step 4: Treat context as a cache and make tools async

The Router can't hold everything, so the essay treats context like a cache:

  • Inline what's likely needed: IDs, short summaries, neighboring messages.
  • Spill the rest: truncate it and leave a pointer the agent can follow.

Stable IDs on Triggers, Threads and Workers form a reference graph the authors call a "Chain of Recall." The agent hops from a Trigger to its Thread to the Worker that handled it, which gives it multi-hop recall without a giant prompt.

Then go full-duplex. Replace a blocking run() tool with async start() and stop(). start() returns "Started" right away, and the result arrives later as a new event. That's what lets the agent take your next instruction while the last one is still running. The essay says DeepSeek Harness implements this but doesn't enable it by default.

Finally, make replies channel-aware. Their tested rule caps IM replies at 100 words, while GitHub, email and docs get structured, dense write-ups.

It also enables speculative execution: in their user group, a "silently reproduce and fix" policy delivers only a confirmed simple fix and otherwise stays quiet.

Step 5: Separate compute, state and environments

Run the agent loop in stateless cloud containers and keep session state in a database. Environments stay where they are: each machine runs a lightweight daemon, which the essay calls BYOM (Bring Your Own Machine). A crashed loop restarts anywhere and reloads its state, while repos stay on their machines.

The essay points to Anthropic's "Scaling Managed Agents: Decoupling the brain from the hands" as the same idea, aimed at managed sandboxes rather than your own machines.

Step 6: Add a Watchdog

The Watchdog is a separate session on a schedule, outside the main system. It handles API errors and asks a model whether each Worker is making progress or drifting. Maintainers can also ask it directly why something failed. Keep it outside the Router's process so a stuck Router can't take its monitor down.

What the experiments showed

The authors ran about 300 chat and CI messages containing about 20 work requests, simulated the coding with a timer, and ran each setup 5 times. They call the results "indicative only."

Setup p50 (min) p95 (min) Cache-read tokens per run Super-agent 12.4 15.7 23.2M Without Thread pass-through 12.6 15.5 31.8M Single session + subagent tool, neutral prompt 20.4 29.5 6.1M Single session, delegation-first prompt 13.8 29.0 10.8M

Two findings stand out. With a neutral prompt, the single session never delegated in 5 runs, so its p95 was nearly double the super-agent's. A delegation-first prompt fixed the median but not the tail. The super-agent costs more tokens than a single session, so you're trading tokens for latency and attention.

A second test loaded the Router alone. As Triggers rose from 1 to 40 per minute, batch size grew from 1.0 to 2.8 and time per request went from 2.5 s to 3.9 s, while time per decision fell from 6.4 s to 1.6 s. Batching is what keeps a single Router from becoming the bottleneck early.

Test your Trigger intake with Apidog CLI

Every Trigger starts life as an HTTP request hitting your intake endpoint, so that endpoint is the first thing worth testing. If it drops a PR comment or assigns a new thread_id to each event, Thread routing breaks and every follow-up goes back through the Router. Let your coding agent write and run that test with Apidog CLI.

npm install -g apidog-cli@latest
apidog auth login --with-token 
npx -y skills add https://apidog.com   # pick your agent when prompted

Then give your agent one [REDACTED PROMPT]
In Apidog project , create POST /triggers/github for a GitHub
pull_request_review_comment webhook. Add a test case that sends two
comments on the same PR and asserts: status 202, a trigger_id in the
body, and the same thread_id both times. Run it against staging and
summarize any failures.


The agent reads each payload schema, validates its JSON, writes the endpoint and the case, and runs it:


bash
apidog cli-schema get endpoint-create
apidog cli-schema validate endpoint-create --file endpoint.json
apidog endpoint create --project --file endpoint.json
apidog cli-schema get test-case-create
apidog cli-schema validate test-case-create --file case.json
apidog test-case create --project --file case.json
apidog run --test-case --project -e -r cli,json




The same `apidog run` call with `-r junit` drops into your pipeline; see [Apidog CLI in CI/CD](http://apidog.com/blog/apidog-cli-ci-cd-pipeline?utm_source=dev.to&utm_medium=wanda&utm_content=n8n-post-automation). If your agent is DeepSeek Harness itself, follow [this setup guide](http://apidog.com/blog/apidog-cli-in-deepseek-harness?utm_source=dev.to&utm_medium=wanda&utm_content=n8n-post-automation); for Claude Code, use [this one](http://apidog.com/blog/apidog-cli-in-claude-code?utm_source=dev.to&utm_medium=wanda&utm_content=n8n-post-automation). Apidog's Free plan covers up to 4 users.

## Open problems

The essay lists what isn't solved:

- **Scaling the Router** and choosing a Worker topology as load grows.
- **Long-term memory** beyond the Chain of Recall.
- **UX without sessions:** steering an agent with no single chat window.
- **Context boundaries and agent-to-agent protocols**, where [A2A](http://apidog.com/blog/what-is-agent2agent-a2a?utm_source=dev.to&utm_medium=wanda&utm_content=n8n-post-automation) is one candidate.
- **Security.** A prompt injection that reaches the cloud loop could reach every connected machine, and credentials in context can leak. The authors want agents to use credentials without ever seeing them.

## FAQ

**Is the super-agent a DeepSeek Harness feature I can turn on?** No. The essay describes architecture. Parts exist in the `dsh-superagent-prototype` plugin, which the authors say is not an official DeepSeek product. Full-duplex tools are implemented but off by default.

**Why does the Router use a lighter model?** It only dispatches and talks to people; it never executes tasks or needs Bash. Workers do the heavy reasoning with the strongest model.

**How is a super-agent different from an agent team?** A team lead splits one coupled task into parts. The Router dispatches independent tasks. A Worker can run its own agent team inside the super-agent.

**What is Thread pass-through?** Follow-up events on a PR, IM topic or email chain go straight to the Worker that owns that Thread, skipping the Router. Removing it raised token use by about 37% in their test.

**Does a super-agent save tokens?** Not against a single session. It used 23.2M cache-read tokens per run versus 6.1M to 10.8M, in exchange for a p95 of 15.7 minutes instead of about 29.

items.title: Inside the OnePassApps Support Desk: 23 Areas, 2,000-Character Bug Reports, and a Hidden App Catalogue
items.summary: I work on OnePassApps, so this is our own product, and everything below is a measurement of the live site at app.onepassapps.com/support, taken on 4 November 2026 - signed out, in one browser, on one build. Most support pages are a textarea and a Send button. Ours is a small workflow: three tabs, four fields, two dropdowns, a character counter, and a "what we store" note that tells you what happens to what you type. I opened every part of it and wrote down what it actually says, because no channel here has covered the support desk itself. The three tabs The page opens with the headline "Let's sort it out." and the line "Help, bug reports and feedback, all in one place." Below that are three tabs: New request - the form My requests - the list of what you have sent Report a bug - a different, smaller form Two of them are worth reading carefully. The request form, field by field How can we help? is the first section, and its first control is a dropdown labelled "I'd like to…". It opens to seven options, and the default is "Help or question": Help or question / Report a bug / Billing / Account or sign-in / Privacy or data / Share feedback / Suggest a feature That first dropdown is the whole routing table for a support request. "Billing" is a peer of "Report a bug", and "Privacy or data" is a peer of "Share feedback" - so the desk sorts a refund question and a "your tool uploaded my file" question through the same seven-item list, not through separate inboxes. Replies to is a required email field with the placeholder you@example.com . Under it sits the sentence that decides who can follow a request: Sign in to keep requests with your account. Guest tracking is saved only in this browser. Subject is optional - the page says "Optional" next to it - with the placeholder "A short summary". Your message is required, and it carries a live counter that read 0 / 5,000 on an empty page. I typed into it and the counter moved with me: thirty characters in, it read 30 / 5,000 . So the limit is five thousand characters, counted as you type. Under the box, the page says: "Leave out passwords and private details." App & other details is a collapsed section. Opening it adds two dropdowns and nothing else: App or area - defaults to "OnePassApps" How much is it affecting you? - defaults to "Minor issue or question", and opens to four levels: "I cannot continue", "Something is not working", "Minor issue or question", "Suggestion or idea" Then the line "Sent to OnePassApps support only." and a Send request button. The dropdown nobody expects: 23 areas "App or area" is the interesting control, because it lists twenty-three names - and they are not the nine apps the home page counts. I read the full list off the open dropdown: OnePassApps, NewsFlow, MovieMatcherAI, PDF Organiser, CV Builder, Email Signature Builder, Chart Maker, Subtitle Workbench, Browser Teleprompter, Screen & Cinema Planner, Label & Card Maker, Social Preview Designer, Citation Formatter, Calendar Maker, Password Generator, Word Counter, Focus Timer, QR Code Maker, Ambient Noise Mixer, Time Zone Planner, Invoice Maker, Signature Maker, Screen Recorder. Twenty-three areas, against a home page that counts nine apps. The home page's four counters read All 9 , Live 2 , Tools 0 and Studios 7 , and its grid holds the two hosted apps and the seven studios. So I checked what those extra names are. Outside the browser, plain HTTPS requests: Fourteen of them answer HTTP 200 at /apps/ , each with its own title and its own meta description. CV Builder - Create and print a resume - OnePassApps . QR Code Maker - Static QR codes for links, Wi-Fi and contacts - OnePassApps . Chart Maker - CSV to bar, line and scatter charts - OnePassApps . Different titles, different byte counts - not one page served twenty times. Six of them answer 404 under the slugs I tried: PDF Organiser, Email Signature Builder, Browser Teleprompter, Screen & Cinema Planner, Label & Card Maker and Social Preview Designer. I tried both /apps/ and /studios/ and two spellings each; the paths may simply be different from the names. Here is the part that matters, and it is not what the status codes say. Those 200 pages carry noindex, nofollow , none of them appear in sitemap.xml (16 URLs, none of them these), and when I opened /apps/cv-builder in the browser, the running app did not show a CV Builder - it sent the visitor to the home page. The served HTML has the title and description; the app shell has no route for it. Which makes the support dropdown the widest catalogue of OnePassApps apps anywhere on the site - wider than the app grid, wider than the nav menu, wider than the sitemap. The desk can take a request about a QR Code Maker that the rest of the product does not currently show you. "My requests", and what it means to have sent something The second tab is titled "My requests", sits under a small heading that reads "IN THIS BROWSER", and on an empty account it says: No requests yet Your reports and replies will appear here. There is a "Refresh requests" button next to it, and the same guest-tracking sentence as the form. The "How support works" panel on the form side is three numbered notes, and the third one is the one worth reading twice: 01 Before you write - The Help centre covers every app, billing, privacy and troubleshooting. The app guides walk through each app. 02 What we store - We store your message and contact email in our support system. 03 Replies - Replies appear under My requests. Guest tracking is saved only in this browser. Clearing site data removes that access, but does not delete the request. Keep your request reference: from another browser, email info@onepassapps.com with it. Sign in to keep requests with your account. That is a specific promise and a specific limitation. The request itself is not deleted when you clear site data - you lose the thread, not the ticket - and the way back in is a reference you are told to keep. Underneath the form: "Can't use this form, or can't sign in? Email info@onepassapps.com ." "Report a bug" is a different form The third tab opens a dialog rather than a page, and it is not the request form with a different title. It has a What happened? field with a 0 / 2,000 counter - two thousand characters, not five - an optional What you expected field, a collapsed Include technical details section, and a Report as control with two choices: With replies Anonymous There is an Email for replies field next to it. So a bug report can be filed anonymously with no email address at all, which the general request form cannot do - there, the email is required. That asymmetry is deliberate and worth stating: the general request form asks who to reply to, the bug form lets you decline to say. Both forms carry the same instruction, in slightly different words: "Leave out passwords and private details." on the request form, "Keep passwords and private details out." on the bug form. Two small things that are easy to miss A direct link can pick the category for you. The home page's plans band links "Contact support about billing or a refund" to /support?kind=billing , and that query string does what it says - I opened it and the "I'd like to…" dropdown was already set to "Billing" rather than "Help or question". The support page is deliberately out of the index. Its robots meta reads noindex, nofollow , and it is not in sitemap.xml . It is still reachable and linkable - the home page's plans band links straight into it with Contact support about billing or a refund - but it is not something the site asks a crawler to list. Honest limits One build, one browser, one day (4 November 2026), signed out. I did not sign in, so anything behind an account - stored requests, replies, the reference history - was not seen. I did not send a request. Everything above is what the page does before you press "Send request"; what happens afterwards is the app's side of it, and I did not test it. The character counters were read on an empty field and once at thirty characters. I did not paste five thousand characters to find the ceiling. The fourteen 200 responses are server responses. What a person sees at those URLs in a browser is the home page, because the app shell has no route for them. Six of the twenty area names did not resolve under the slugs I guessed. That is a statement about my guesses, not proof that those pages do not exist. If you want to see the desk itself, it is at app.onepassapps.com/support , and the per-app walkthroughs are at app.onepassapps.com/guides . I work on OnePassApps. This is our own product and every number above came from our own live build on the day I wrote it.

The request form, field by field

QR Code Maker - Static QR codes for links, Wi-Fi and contacts - OnePassApps. Chart Maker - CSV to bar, line and scatter charts - OnePassApps. "My requests", and what it means to have sent something

No requests yet
Your reports and replies will appear here.

There is a "Refresh requests" button next to it, and the same guest-tracking sentence as the form.

01 Before you write - The Help centre covers every app, billing, privacy and troubleshooting. The app guides walk through each app.
02 What we store - We store your message and contact email in our support system.
03 Replies - Replies appear under My requests. Guest tracking is saved only in this browser. Clearing site data removes that access, but does not delete the request. Keep your request reference: from another browser, email info@onepassapps.com with it. Sign in to keep requests with your account.

items.title: Prompt Caching, Explained: How Claude Reuses Your Prompt Prefix — and When It Doesn't Pay Off
items.summary: If you build anything that talks to Claude more than once — a chatbot, a coding agent, a document Q&A tool — you are probably paying to process the same text over and over again. Every API request is stateless: the model re-reads your system prompt, your tool definitions, and the whole conversation history each time. Prompt caching is Anthropic's answer to that waste. It lets the API reuse a previously processed prefix of your prompt instead of processing it again. This is not a different model or a new endpoint. It is a way of marking part of your request as reusable. Here is how it works, what it costs, and where it quietly stops working. What gets cached: a prefix, not a paragraph A cache entry covers the start of your request, up to a breakpoint you mark. Anthropic's docs describe the prefix as being built in a fixed order: tool definitions first, then the system prompt, then the message history. Everything from the very first token up to and including your breakpoint becomes one cacheable unit. That ordering is the whole design discipline. Put the content that rarely changes at the beginning — your tools, your system instructions, your background documents, your few-shot examples — and put the thing that changes every request at the end. If the variable part sits inside the cached prefix, the prefix is different on every request and nothing is ever reused. Two ways to turn it on Automatic caching is the simplest start: add a single cache_control field at the top level of your request, and the system places the breakpoint on the last cacheable block for you. As a multi-turn conversation grows, the breakpoint moves forward automatically, so each new request reads the earlier turns from cache and writes only the newest exchange. Explicit breakpoints give you finer control. You place cache_control directly on individual content blocks — for example, one breakpoint after your system prompt and another after a large reference document that updates daily. You can define up to 4 breakpoints in a request, which also helps when a long conversation grows past the 20-block lookback window the docs describe: each breakpoint gets its own backward search for a prior cache entry. Breakpoints themselves cost nothing. You pay only for cache writes, cache reads, and the uncached tokens in each request. What it costs By default, a cache entry lives for 5 minutes, and reading it refreshes that lifetime at no extra charge. The lifetime is measured from the start of the request that writes or reads the entry, not from the end of the response — so a response that takes 4 minutes to stream leaves only about 1 minute for the follow-up to reuse the same prefix. The price structure, per Anthropic's documentation: Cache writes (5-minute TTL) cost 25% more than base input tokens. Cache reads cost 10% of the base input price for most models, with exceptions: 0.025x for Claude Fable 5.1 and Claude Mythos 5.1, and 0.05x for Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Sonnet 5.5. A 1-hour TTL is available at 2x the base input price for writes. A concrete example from the pricing table: for Claude Sonnet 4.6, base input is $3 per million tokens, a 5-minute cache write is $3.75, a 1-hour write is $6, and a cache read is $0.30. So the second request that reuses a large prefix is dramatically cheaper than the first — but the first request is slightly more expensive than it would be without caching. Caching only pays off when the prefix is actually reused. The minimums and the traps Not every prompt is eligible. items.summary_html:
If you build anything that talks to Claude more than once — a chatbot, a coding agent, a document Q&A tool — you are probably paying to process the same text over and over again. Every API request is stateless: the model re-reads your system prompt, your tool definitions, and the whole conversation history each time. Prompt caching is Anthropic's answer to that waste. It lets the API reuse a previously processed prefix of your prompt instead of processing it again.

This is not a different model or a new endpoint. It is a way of marking part of your request as reusable. Here is how it works, what it costs, and where it quietly stops working.

What gets cached: a prefix, not a paragraph

A cache entry covers the start of your request, up to a breakpoint you mark. Anthropic's docs describe the prefix as being built in a fixed order: tool definitions first, then the system prompt, then the message history. Everything from the very first token up to and including your breakpoint becomes one cacheable unit.

That ordering is the whole design discipline. Put the content that rarely changes at the beginning — your tools, your system instructions, your background documents, your few-shot examples — and put the thing that changes every request at the end. If the variable part sits inside the cached prefix, the prefix is different on every request and nothing is ever reused.

Two ways to turn it on

Automatic caching is the simplest start: add a single cache_control field at the top level of your request, and the system places the breakpoint on the last cacheable block for you. As a multi-turn conversation grows, the breakpoint moves forward automatically, so each new request reads the earlier turns from cache and writes only the newest exchange.

Explicit breakpoints give you finer control. You place cache_control directly on individual content blocks — for example, one breakpoint after your system prompt and another after a large reference document that updates daily. You can define up to 4 breakpoints in a request, which also helps when a long conversation grows past the 20-block lookback window the docs describe: each breakpoint gets its own backward search for a prior cache entry.

Breakpoints themselves cost nothing. You pay only for cache writes, cache reads, and the uncached tokens in each request.

What it costs

By default, a cache entry lives for 5 minutes, and reading it refreshes that lifetime at no extra charge. The lifetime is measured from the start of the request that writes or reads the entry, not from the end of the response — so a response that takes 4 minutes to stream leaves only about 1 minute for the follow-up to reuse the same prefix.

The price structure, per Anthropic's documentation:

  • Cache writes (5-minute TTL) cost 25% more than base input tokens.
  • Cache reads cost 10% of the base input price for most models, with exceptions: 0.025x for Claude Fable 5.1 and Claude Mythos 5.1, and 0.05x for Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Sonnet 5.5.
  • A 1-hour TTL is available at 2x the base input price for writes.

A concrete example from the pricing table: for Claude Sonnet 4.6, base input is $3 per million tokens, a 5-minute cache write is $3.75, a 1-hour write is $6, and a cache read is $0.30. So the second request that reuses a large prefix is dramatically cheaper than the first — but the first request is slightly more expensive than it would be without caching. Caching only pays off when the prefix is actually reused.

The minimums and the traps

Not every prompt is eligible. There is a minimum cacheable prompt length, which varies by model — for example, 1,024 tokens for Claude Sonnet 4.6 and Sonnet 4.5, and 512 tokens for newer models such as Claude Sonnet 5.5, Opus 5.5, and Haiku 5.5. A short system prompt will simply never be cached, silently.

The most common failure mode is documented with unusual clarity: a breakpoint placed on a block that changes every request — say, a message containing a fresh timestamp — produces a different prefix hash each time. The lookback walks backward looking for entries that prior requests actually wrote, and since no prior request wrote an entry at an earlier position, there is no hit. You pay for a fresh cache write on every request and never get a read. The fix is to move the breakpoint to the last block that stays identical across requests.

Two more rules worth knowing:

  • The cache is per model. Switching models mid-conversation starts cold.
  • Automatic and explicit breakpoints can conflict. If the last block already has an explicit breakpoint with a different TTL, the API returns a 400 error, and if 4 explicit breakpoints already exist there is no slot left for automatic caching.
A practical checklist
  1. Order your request: static content first, varying content last.
  2. Start with automatic caching — one top-level cache_control field — unless you have sections that change at different frequencies.
  3. Put explicit breakpoints at the end of each stable section, never on a block containing a timestamp or per-request data.
  4. Check that your stable prefix clears the model's minimum token threshold; otherwise nothing is cached at all.
  5. If your turns are long, add a second breakpoint so a growing conversation does not push the last cache write outside the 20-block lookback window.
  6. Choose the 5-minute TTL for active conversations and the 1-hour TTL only when gaps between requests are long enough to justify the 2x write price.

Prompt caching does not make the model smarter, and it does not change what the model outputs. It just stops you from paying full price to re-read the same instructions for the hundredth time. Used with the prefix discipline above, that is one of the cheapest wins available in a production LLM app.

All pricing and behavior details in this article are from Anthropic's prompt caching documentation: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-caching — re-check the page before relying on a number, since pricing and minimums change.
