items.title: 2,000 TripAdvisor reviews in 62 seconds for one cent: what one Times Square hotel's guests actually complain about
items.summary: TripAdvisor shows a hotel's all-time score at the top of the page. For an old hotel with 18,000 reviews, that number mostly describes stays from years ago. If you want to know what guests say now, you need the recent reviews themselves, in a table. So we pulled them. One run of our TripAdvisor Reviews Scraper on Apify, pointed at the Hotel Edison Times Square, asking for 2,000 reviews: Time: 62 seconds. Cost: $0.0096 of compute on our side. A user pays $0.50 per 1,000 reviews on the Starter tier, so this run is $1.00 for anyone else. Coverage: 2,000 reviews from 12 Dec 2024 to 3 Nov 2026, plus one row for the hotel itself. Every number below comes from that one run. Reviews are written by members of the public, so this post shows counts only: no reviewer names and no quotes from reviews. The input { "startUrls" : [ { "url" : "https://www.tripadvisor.com/Hotel_Review-g60763-d93437-Reviews-Hotel_Edison_Times_Square-New_York_City_New_York.html" } ], "maxReviewsPerPlace" : 2000 } Any TripAdvisor review page works the same way: hotels, restaurants and attractions, on any TripAdvisor country site. Filters are optional: ratings (for example only 1 and 2 stars), reviewsSince , languages , tripTypes (family, couples, solo, business, friends), reviewsContaining and sortBy . From Python: from apify_client import ApifyClient client = ApifyClient ( " YOUR_APIFY_TOKEN " ) run = client . actor ( " locaihost/tripadvisor-reviews " ). call ( run_input = { " startUrls " : [{ " url " : " https://www.tripadvisor.com/Hotel_Review-g60763-d93437-Reviews-Hotel_Edison_Times_Square-New_York_City_New_York.html " }], " maxReviewsPerPlace " : 2000 , }) rows = list ( client . dataset ( run [ " defaultDatasetId " ]). iterate_items ()) reviews = [ r for r in rows if r [ " type " ] == " review " ] Each review row has the rating, title, full text, language (and whether TripAdvisor machine-translated it), published date, travel month, trip type, sub-ratings when given, helpful votes, photo count and the hotel's reply. Reviewer names are off by default. The place row carries the address, coordinates, all-time rating and histogram, sub-scores, the "#169 of 529 hotels" ranking, amenities, and three numbers computed from the reviews you collected: owner reply rate, average reply lag and the rating over the last 90 days. Finding 1: the all-time score hides two good years Reviews Average 5 stars All time (TripAdvisor's own histogram) 18,836 3.9 40% Latest 2,000 (Dec 2024 to Nov 2026) 2,000 4.43 71% The headline 3.9 is dragged down by older stays: 2,482 of the hotel's one and two-star reviews are in the all-time histogram, and only 176 of them are in the last two years. Month by month, the recent average sits between 4.18 (September 2026) and 4.67 (April 2025), with no trend down. If you compare hotels by their all-time score, an older property that has improved looks worse than it is. A 90-day or 12-month average from the raw reviews is fairer, and it's one column in the output ( ratingLast90d : 4.35 over 250 reviews here). Finding 2: who is happiest Trip type Reviews Average Solo 93 4.78 Friends 256 4.68 Family 620 4.58 Couples 262 4.47 Business 124 4.34 Not given 645 4.14 Business travellers rate it lowest of the groups that say why they came. Reviewers who don't pick a trip type are the least happy of all, which is common: an angry reviewer fills in fewer optional fields. Finding 3: what the bad reviews are about We split the reviews into 176 low (1 or 2 stars) and 1,701 high (4 or 5 stars) and counted how many in each group mention a word at least once (whole words only): Mentioned Low reviews High reviews noise / noisy 23% 7% bathroom 26% 8% old / dated / outdated 20% 5% check-in 17% 8% window 16% 1% price / expensive / overpriced 18% 6% rude 12% 0% fee / fees 11% 1% air conditioning / AC 11% 2% dirty 9% 0% staff 44% 54% location 34% 54% clean 15% 33% The pattern is clear even with simple word counts. Happy guests talk about the staff and the location. Unhappy guests talk about the room itself (bathroom, noise through the windows, an old building, the air conditioning) and about the front desk (check-in, rude, fees). "Staff" shows up in both groups, because staff are the reason for both the best and the worst reviews. This is the cheapest version of the analysis. With the full text in a dataframe, the next step is an embedding or topic model over the 176 low reviews, which takes a few seconds on a laptop. Finding 4: the hotel answers almost everything 1,991 of the 2,000 reviews have a reply from the hotel (99.6%), including 175 of the 176 low ones, and the average reply comes 4.6 days after the review. That's a well-run reply process. For a competitor analysis, reply rate and reply lag are two of the most telling columns: they show which hotels have someone watching their reviews. What it doesn't do It reads what a logged-out visitor can see. A list stops at about 10,000 reviews; for bigger places, run it per star rating to go deeper. Machine-translated reviews are marked ( machineTranslated ). 161 of these 2,000 were translations; filter them out with languages if you only want originals. It doesn't name staff. Names in the hotel's replies are replaced with [name removed] . Try it The Actor is locaihost/tripadvisor-reviews on the Apify Store: $0.50 per 1,000 reviews and $1 per 1,000 places on the Starter tier, cheaper on the higher tiers, and links that aren't a TripAdvisor place are never charged. It also works from AI agents through Apify's MCP server, so "pull the last 500 reviews of these 10 hotels and tell me what the one-star ones have in common" is one tool call away. If you run it and something looks wrong, open an issue on the Actor page and we'll fix it the same day.

TripAdvisor shows a hotel's all-time score at the top of the page. For an old hotel with 18,000 reviews, that number mostly describes stays from years ago. If you want to know what guests say now, you need the recent reviews themselves, in a table.

So we pulled them. One run of our TripAdvisor Reviews Scraper on Apify, pointed at the Hotel Edison Times Square, asking for 2,000 reviews:

  • Time: 62 seconds.
  • Cost: $0.0096 of compute on our side. A user pays $0.50 per 1,000 reviews on the Starter tier, so this run is $1.00 for anyone else.
  • Coverage: 2,000 reviews from 12 Dec 2024 to 3 Nov 2026, plus one row for the hotel itself.

Every number below comes from that one run. Reviews are written by members of the public, so this post shows counts only: no reviewer names and no quotes from reviews.

The input 
{
  "startUrls": [
    { "url": "https://www.tripadvisor.com/Hotel_Review-g60763-d93437-Reviews-Hotel_Edison_Times_Square-New_York_City_New_York.html" }
  ],
  "maxReviewsPerPlace": 2000
}

Any TripAdvisor review page works the same way: hotels, restaurants and attractions, on any TripAdvisor country site. Filters are optional: ratings (for example only 1 and 2 stars), reviewsSince, languages, tripTypes (family, couples, solo, business, friends), reviewsContaining and sortBy.

From Python:

from apify_client import ApifyClient

client = ApifyClient("YOUR_APIFY_TOKEN")
run = client.actor("locaihost/tripadvisor-reviews").call(run_input={
    "startUrls": [{"url": "https://www.tripadvisor.com/Hotel_Review-g60763-d93437-Reviews-Hotel_Edison_Times_Square-New_York_City_New_York.html"}],
    "maxReviewsPerPlace": 2000,
})
rows = list(client.dataset(run["defaultDatasetId"]).iterate_items())
reviews = [r for r in rows if r["type"] == "review"]

Each review row has the rating, title, full text, language (and whether TripAdvisor machine-translated it), published date, travel month, trip type, sub-ratings when given, helpful votes, photo count and the hotel's reply. Reviewer names are off by default. The place row carries the address, coordinates, all-time rating and histogram, sub-scores, the "#169 of 529 hotels" ranking, amenities, and three numbers computed from the reviews you collected: owner reply rate, average reply lag and the rating over the last 90 days.

Finding 1: the all-time score hides two good years
Reviews Average 5 stars All time (TripAdvisor's own histogram) 18,836 3.9 40% Latest 2,000 (Dec 2024 to Nov 2026) 2,000 4.43 71%

The headline 3.9 is dragged down by older stays: 2,482 of the hotel's one and two-star reviews are in the all-time histogram, and only 176 of them are in the last two years. Month by month, the recent average sits between 4.18 (September 2026) and 4.67 (April 2025), with no trend down.

If you compare hotels by their all-time score, an older property that has improved looks worse than it is. A 90-day or 12-month average from the raw reviews is fairer, and it's one column in the output (ratingLast90d: 4.35 over 250 reviews here).

Finding 2: who is happiest
Trip type Reviews Average Solo 93 4.78 Friends 256 4.68 Family 620 4.58 Couples 262 4.47 Business 124 4.34 Not given 645 4.14

Business travellers rate it lowest of the groups that say why they came. Reviewers who don't pick a trip type are the least happy of all, which is common: an angry reviewer fills in fewer optional fields.

Finding 3: what the bad reviews are about

We split the reviews into 176 low (1 or 2 stars) and 1,701 high (4 or 5 stars) and counted how many in each group mention a word at least once (whole words only):

Mentioned Low reviews High reviews noise / noisy 23% 7% bathroom 26% 8% old / dated / outdated 20% 5% check-in 17% 8% window 16% 1% price / expensive / overpriced 18% 6% rude 12% 0% fee / fees 11% 1% air conditioning / AC 11% 2% dirty 9% 0% staff 44% 54% location 34% 54% clean 15% 33%

The pattern is clear even with simple word counts. Happy guests talk about the staff and the location. Unhappy guests talk about the room itself (bathroom, noise through the windows, an old building, the air conditioning) and about the front desk (check-in, rude, fees). "Staff" shows up in both groups, because staff are the reason for both the best and the worst reviews.

This is the cheapest version of the analysis. With the full text in a dataframe, the next step is an embedding or topic model over the 176 low reviews, which takes a few seconds on a laptop.

Finding 4: the hotel answers almost everything

1,991 of the 2,000 reviews have a reply from the hotel (99.6%), including 175 of the 176 low ones, and the average reply comes 4.6 days after the review. That's a well-run reply process. For a competitor analysis, reply rate and reply lag are two of the most telling columns: they show which hotels have someone watching their reviews.

What it doesn't do
  • It reads what a logged-out visitor can see. A list stops at about 10,000 reviews; for bigger places, run it per star rating to go deeper.
  • Machine-translated reviews are marked (machineTranslated). 161 of these 2,000 were translations; filter them out with languages if you only want originals.
  • It doesn't name staff. Names in the hotel's replies are replaced with [name removed].
Try it

The Actor is locaihost/tripadvisor-reviews on the Apify Store: $0.50 per 1,000 reviews and $1 per 1,000 places on the Starter tier, cheaper on the higher tiers, and links that aren't a TripAdvisor place are never charged. items.title: Turning Video into Line Art in the Browser with WebGL 2 and Sobel
items.summary: Depth maps and line art preserve different parts of a video. Depth describes spatial relationships; contours emphasize shape, composition, and visible changes in pose. After adding depth-video conversion to Timeline Studio , my open-source browser video editor, I added a line-art asset generator. This version runs locally with WebGL 2 and Sobel edge extraction. It does not download or run a neural line-art model. Source code · Try the editor Here is how the image-processing pipeline connects to actual video editing: previews, trimmed clips, speed curves, source audio, encoding, and cancellation. Two passes on the GPU The pipeline is deliberately small: Image or decoded video frame | Grayscale + 3x3 smoothing | Intermediate GPU texture | Sobel + soft threshold | Output canvas | PNG or WebM The smoothing pass renders into a texture attached to a framebuffer. The edge pass samples that texture and draws to the output canvas. Intermediate pixels stay on the GPU rather than being read back into JavaScript between passes. Shader programs, buffers, textures, and the framebuffer are reused across frames. That reduces setup work, although decoding and encoding still contribute to total processing time. Convert to luminance, then smooth The shader computes a weighted RGB luminance: float gray ( vec2 p ) { return dot ( texture ( source , p ). rgb , vec3 ( 0 . 2126 , 0 . 7152 , 0 . 0722 ) ); } The first pass uses this weighted 3x3 kernel, divided by 16: 1 2 1 2 4 2 1 2 1 Smoothing suppresses some high-frequency texture before edge extraction. It is a tradeoff: small details can also become weaker. Because detection operates on luminance, different colors with similar luminance may produce weak boundaries. Conversely, a shadow or reflection can produce a strong edge without marking an object boundary. Extract Sobel gradients The second pass estimates horizontal and vertical gradients: Gx Gy -1 0 1 -1 -2 -1 -2 0 2 0 0 0 -1 0 1 1 2 1 Their combined magnitude becomes the edge strength: float gradient = length ( vec2 ( c + 2 . 0 * f + i - a - 2 . 0 * e - g , g + 2 . 0 * h + i - a - 2 . 0 * b - c )); The letters represent neighboring luminance samples. Each output pixel performs the same local calculation, which maps naturally to a fragment shader. Make the parameters useful The inspector exposes detail, line weight, and inversion. Defaults are 55% detail, 1x line weight, and black lines on white. Detail maps to an edge threshold: float threshold = mix ( 0 . 42 , 0 . 035 , detail / 100 . 0 ); float ink = smoothstep ( threshold * 0 . 5 , threshold , gradient ); float value = inverted ? ink : 1 . 0 - ink ; Higher detail lowers the threshold, retaining weaker edges. The soft threshold avoids an abrupt binary transition around the cutoff. For busy footage, increasing detail can make the result less useful by retaining background texture. Line weight changes the sampling distance. It uses the longest dimension as a 1080px reference: const scaledThickness = thickness * Math . max ( width , height ) / 1080 ; This helps keep the edge-sampling scale comparable across output sizes. It is not morphological dilation: changing the sampling distance also changes which details respond. The initial blur itself remains a one-pixel 3x3 neighborhood. Preview and asset generation share one renderer Both paths call the same implementation: const renderer = createLineArtRenderer ( canvas , width , height ); renderer . draw ( media , options ); // Release resources when finished: renderer . dispose (); The preview redraws a sampled frame when parameters or the local playhead time change. Asset generation traverses output frames through that same renderer. Sharing the implementation reduces differences in thresholds, sampling, and inversion between preview and generated assets. It does not make processing instantaneous. Output dimensions preserve aspect ratio, cap the longest edge at 1080 by default, avoid enlarging smaller media, and normalize dimensions to even numbers. Video has to follow the timeline's clock A selected clip may already be trimmed or retimed. Sampling the original file from zero would produce the wrong result. There are separate coordinates for output time, clip-local time, and source-media time. For constant speed: sourceTime = sourceIn + clipLocalTime * speed For speed curves, the implementation reuses the editor's mapping: getVisualSourceTime ( segment , localTime ) The generator outputs 24 fps. Each local sample time is i / 24; it is mapped to source time before decoding the frame. The processed frame is then encoded at its output timestamp. Output frame time | Source-time mapping, including trim and retiming | Decode source frame -> draw contours -> encode output Mediabunny handles media input and timestamp-based canvas sampling. The final frame duration is limited to the remaining clip duration. 24 fps is the output rate, not a claim of real-time generation speed. Actual throughput depends on the browser, hardware, source media, and encoder. Normalize still-image orientation One integration detail had nothing to do with Sobel: image orientation. The image path decodes a Blob to an ImageBitmap, then draws it to a 2D canvas before uploading it to WebGL. ImageBitmap does not follow the same UNPACK_FLIP_Y_WEBGL behavior as the other upload path, so the intermediate canvas normalizes orientation. Without that step, still images and video frames could disagree about which side is up. Encode a reusable asset, with corresponding source audio Images become PNG. Videos become WebM using VP9 at approximately 4 Mbps. When corresponding source audio exists, the output uses Opus at 192 kbps. Audio preparation reuses the editor's source-audio and offline-mixing helpers so trimming and retiming follow the selected segment. This preserves the segment's corresponding source sound; it does not mix every music and narration track from the whole project. The completed asset goes to My assets . It is not automatically inserted into the timeline, making it possible to retain the original and compare versions before placement. Cancellation includes cleanup An AbortController carries cancellation through source reading, frame processing, and output finalization. The renderer releases its textures, framebuffer, shaders, programs, and vertex buffer. Media input resources are disposed, and encoding is canceled when necessary. Frame processing reports progress up to 99%. Finalization and the asset commit must finish before the UI reports completion. Processing the last frame is not the same as having a usable saved file. What structural reference means here Depth video and contour video provide complementary reference assets: Asset Emphasizes Depth video Relative depth and foreground/background layout Line-art video Visible contours, composition, and changes in shape A downstream generation workflow can use these only if it accepts the corresponding conditioning input and its preprocessing, timing, resolution, and frame-rate requirements are satisfied. This feature creates the reference asset. It does not imply automatic integration with every image or video generator, nor guarantee that a generator will preserve the desired structure. The current Sobel route also lacks semantic simplification and explicit temporal tracking. Fine textures, noise, and motion can make lines fluctuate across frames. A learned line-art model or additional temporal processing would need separate evaluation rather than being claimed as part of this implementation. Try it or read the code Open Effects -> Line art , select an image or video clip, adjust parameters, and generate the asset. The feature includes 13 interface languages and a mobile layout. Depth maps and line art preserve different parts of a video. Depth describes spatial relationships; contours emphasize shape, composition, and visible changes in pose.

After adding depth-video conversion to Timeline Studio, my open-source browser video editor, I added a line-art asset generator. This version runs locally with WebGL 2 and Sobel edge extraction. It does not download or run a neural line-art model.

Source code · Try the editor

Here is how the image-processing pipeline connects to actual video editing: previews, trimmed clips, speed curves, source audio, encoding, and cancellation.

Two passes on the GPU

The pipeline is deliberately small:

Image or decoded video frame
          |
   Grayscale + 3x3 smoothing
          |
   Intermediate GPU texture
          |
   Sobel + soft threshold
          |
    Output canvas
          |
      PNG or WebM

The smoothing pass renders into a texture attached to a framebuffer. The edge pass samples that texture and draws to the output canvas. Intermediate pixels stay on the GPU rather than being read back into JavaScript between passes.

Shader programs, buffers, textures, and the framebuffer are reused across frames. That reduces setup work, although decoding and encoding still contribute to total processing time.

Convert to luminance, then smooth

The shader computes a weighted RGB luminance:

float gray(vec2 p) {
  return dot(
    texture(source, p).rgb,
    vec3(0.2126, 0.7152, 0.0722)
  );
}

The first pass uses this weighted 3x3 kernel, divided by 16:

1  2  1
2  4  2
1  2  1

Smoothing suppresses some high-frequency texture before edge extraction. It is a tradeoff: small details can also become weaker.

Because detection operates on luminance, different colors with similar luminance may produce weak boundaries. Conversely, a shadow or reflection can produce a strong edge without marking an object boundary.

Extract Sobel gradients

The second pass estimates horizontal and vertical gradients:

Gx                  Gy
-1  0  1            -1 -2 -1
-2  0  2             0  0  0
-1  0  1             1  2  1

Their combined magnitude becomes the edge strength:

float gradient = length(vec2(
  c + 2.0 * f + i - a - 2.0 * e - g,
  g + 2.0 * h + i - a - 2.0 * b - c
));

The letters represent neighboring luminance samples. Each output pixel performs the same local calculation, which maps naturally to a fragment shader.

Make the parameters useful

The inspector exposes detail, line weight, and inversion. Defaults are 55% detail, 1x line weight, and black lines on white.

Detail maps to an edge threshold:

float threshold = mix(0.42, 0.035, detail / 100.0);
float ink = smoothstep(threshold * 0.5, threshold, gradient);
float value = inverted ? ink : 1.0 - ink;

Higher detail lowers the threshold, retaining weaker edges. The soft threshold avoids an abrupt binary transition around the cutoff. For busy footage, increasing detail can make the result less useful by retaining background texture.

Line weight changes the sampling distance. It uses the longest dimension as a 1080px reference:

const scaledThickness =
  thickness * Math.max(width, height) / 1080;

This helps keep the edge-sampling scale comparable across output sizes. It is not morphological dilation: changing the sampling distance also changes which details respond. The initial blur itself remains a one-pixel 3x3 neighborhood.

Preview and asset generation share one renderer

Both paths call the same implementation:

const renderer = createLineArtRenderer(canvas, width, height);
renderer.draw(media, options);
// Release resources when finished:
renderer.dispose();

The preview redraws a sampled frame when parameters or the local playhead time change. Asset generation traverses output frames through that same renderer.

Sharing the implementation reduces differences in thresholds, sampling, and inversion between preview and generated assets. It does not make processing instantaneous.

Output dimensions preserve aspect ratio, cap the longest edge at 1080 by default, avoid enlarging smaller media, and normalize dimensions to even numbers.

Video has to follow the timeline's clock

A selected clip may already be trimmed or retimed. Sampling the original file from zero would produce the wrong result.

There are separate coordinates for output time, clip-local time, and source-media time. For constant speed:

sourceTime = sourceIn + clipLocalTime * speed

For speed curves, the implementation reuses the editor's mapping:

getVisualSourceTime(segment, localTime)

The generator outputs 24 fps. Each local sample time is i / 24; it is mapped to source time before decoding the frame. The processed frame is then encoded at its output timestamp.

Output frame time
       |
Source-time mapping, including trim and retiming
       |
Decode source frame -> draw contours -> encode output

Mediabunny handles media input and timestamp-based canvas sampling. The final frame duration is limited to the remaining clip duration.

24 fps is the output rate, not a claim of real-time generation speed. Actual throughput depends on the browser, hardware, source media, and encoder.

Normalize still-image orientation

One integration detail had nothing to do with Sobel: image orientation.

The image path decodes a Blob to an ImageBitmap, then draws it to a 2D canvas before uploading it to WebGL. ImageBitmap does not follow the same UNPACK_FLIP_Y_WEBGL behavior as the other upload path, so the intermediate canvas normalizes orientation.

Without that step, still images and video frames could disagree about which side is up.

Encode a reusable asset, with corresponding source audio

Images become PNG. Videos become WebM using VP9 at approximately 4 Mbps. When corresponding source audio exists, the output uses Opus at 192 kbps.

Audio preparation reuses the editor's source-audio and offline-mixing helpers so trimming and retiming follow the selected segment. This preserves the segment's corresponding source sound; it does not mix every music and narration track from the whole project.

The completed asset goes to My assets. It is not automatically inserted into the timeline, making it possible to retain the original and compare versions before placement.

Cancellation includes cleanup

An AbortController carries cancellation through source reading, frame processing, and output finalization. The renderer releases its textures, framebuffer, shaders, programs, and vertex buffer. Media input resources are disposed, and encoding is canceled when necessary.

Frame processing reports progress up to 99%. Finalization and the asset commit must finish before the UI reports completion. Processing the last frame is not the same as having a usable saved file.

What structural reference means here

Depth video and contour video provide complementary reference assets:

Asset Emphasizes Depth video Relative depth and foreground/background layout Line-art video Visible contours, composition, and changes in shape

A downstream generation workflow can use these only if it accepts the corresponding conditioning input and its preprocessing, timing, resolution, and frame-rate requirements are satisfied.

This feature creates the reference asset. It does not imply automatic integration with every image or video generator, nor guarantee that a generator will preserve the desired structure.

The current Sobel route also lacks semantic simplification and explicit temporal tracking. Fine textures, noise, and motion can make lines fluctuate across frames. A learned line-art model or additional temporal processing would need separate evaluation rather than being claimed as part of this implementation.

Try it or read the code

Open Effects -> Line art, select an image or video clip, adjust parameters, and generate the asset. The feature includes 13 interface languages and a mobile layout.

Implementation entry points:

  • src/lib/lineArt.js: renderer, source sampling, encoding, and cleanup
  • src/components/LineArtPanel.jsx: preview, controls, and job state
  • src/i18nLineArt.js: localized copy

If you work on browser graphics or video tools, I would welcome difficult examples: busy backgrounds, small contours, and fast motion are particularly useful for understanding where this approach needs improvement.

items.title: Texas just went blue, and the tech bros are sad
items.summary: Tech bros headed to Texas to find redder pastures. Democrats just flipped the governor's mansion and a Senate seat. Elías Valverde II/The Dallas Morning News via Getty Images, Brandon Bell/Getty Images, Jordan Vonderhaar/Bloomberg via Getty Images Texas drew in tech moguls — including many who wanted redder politics than Silicon Valley. Well, it just turned pretty blue. We're starting to see the anger from tech execs trickle out. Texas — with its cowboy hats, slow-smoked barbecue, and de-regulatory stance — was supposed to be the California antidote for tech bros fed up with Silicon Valley's Democratic politics. Well, Texas just got a lot bluer. On Tuesday, during the midterm elections, Texas voters selected Democrats James Talarico for the Senate and Gina Hinojosa for the governor's mansion, despite massive Republican spending backed by Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk . Now, the tech-world frustration is starting to trickle out . "Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now," Musk wrote on X. Jason Calacanis, a tech investor and co-host of the "All-In Podcast," had a similar reaction. "I never expected Texas to turn blue," he wrote on X. "Ugh, I moved here to get away from the left lunacy!" It was clear over the past year that President Trump was going to lead the GOP off the cliff because of ice, the war, tariffs, the other war and inflation. … but I never expected Texas to turn blue 🤯 Ugh, I moved here to get away from the left lunacy! https://t.co/VTFzfXchHp — @jason (@Jason) November 4, 2026 Chamath Palihapitiya, another "All-In" co-host, was more dire during a Tuesday-night livestream. "There's only one thing that sinks the US economy," he said. "That's the AI trade. And the only way to sink the AI trade is to sink the data centers. And the only way to sink the data centers is to sink the power. And all the power that matters right now is in West Texas." Alex Cohen, the Texas-based CEO and cofounder of AI healthcare company Hello Patient, had a blunter response on X: "RIP AI it was fun while it lasted." The Lone Star State had not elected a statewide Democratic candidate since Ann Richards won the governor's race in 1990. Talarico is the first Democrat to win a Texas Senate election since Lloyd Bentsen in 1988. Not everyone in tech is angry at the results. LinkedIn cofounder Reid Hoffman, a prominent donor for Democrats , called the midterm elections, including the Texas results, "an overwhelming wave against Trump and his cronies," in a post on X. As of publication, several outspoken Texas-based tech figures — including David Sacks, Travis Kalanick, and Blockchain co-CEO Lane Kasselman — had not posted about the results. items.title: Happiest Minds Q2 Revenue Rises 12.5%; AI Revenue Figure Remains Undisclosed
items.summary: Happiest Minds Technologies' Generative AI Business Services revenue grew nearly 50% sequentially in Q3 FY26. However, the IT services company did not disclose a separate AI revenue figure in its Q2 FY27 results, despite previously indicating that it planned to report AI and AI-led revenue by the end of Q2 FY27. The company reported revenue of ₹645.43 crore for the quarter ended September 30, up 12.5% year-on-year (YoY) and 2.7% quarter-on-quarter (QoQ). Revenue growth in constant currency terms stood at 6.8% YoY and 2.4% QoQ. Happiest Minds reported earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation (EBITDA) of ₹142.04 crore, up 18.1% YoY. EBITDA margin improved to 21.3% from 20.2% a year earlier. Operating margin increased 22.4% to ₹119.11 crore, while the operating margin percentage rose to 18.5% from 17%. Net profit increased 15.1% YoY to ₹62.19 crore. Adjusted profit after tax (PAT), which excludes exceptional items and amortisation of intangible assets, grew 20.7% to ₹79.11 crore. Sequentially, however, reported PAT declined 8% and adjusted PAT fell 1.8%. EBITDA grew just 0.5% QoQ, against revenue growth of 2.7%. The company incurred an exceptional expense of ₹3.98 crore towards its proposed merger with ITC Infotech during the quarter. Happiest Minds Managing Director Venkatraman Narayanan said, “The proposed combination with ITC Infotech is progressing well and remains on track with our targeted timelines.” The combined entity is expected to have a workforce of more than 19,000 employees, with an aspiration to generate $1 billion in annual revenue by FY28. Happiest Minds added seven clients during the quarter, taking its total to 311 as of September 30. Its workforce stood at 6,466 employees. Trailing 12-month attrition declined to 14.3% from 15.4% in the previous quarter, while utilisation improved to 81.8% from 80.9%. Happiest Minds’ board declared an interim dividend of ₹3.05 per equity share, with a face value of ₹2 for FY27. November 6 is the record date.

items.title: Sarvam AI Launches Prism, a Jev-Like Decision Model Built on Sarvam 105B
items.summary: Sarvam AI has launched Prism, a System 1 decision model built on its Sarvam 105B model, which the company says can return responses in 44 milliseconds while maintaining an average score of 71.8 across three benchmarks. Prism is a LoRA fine-tune of Sarvam 105B. Unlike conventional language models that generate responses token by token, it processes the input in a single forward pass and returns a probability score for each available option. The model’s weights are available on Hugging Face under the Apache 2.0 licence, allowing enterprises to fine-tune it on their own data and deploy it on their infrastructure. Sarvam said Prism can run in FP8 precision on a single GPU with at least 120 GB of memory. It is also available through the Sarvam API. The Bengaluru-based AI startup said Prism was tested against 24 other decision models and recorded the highest average score among models with response times below 100 milliseconds. The tests were conducted on a single NVIDIA B200 GPU. “Prism sets a new point on the Pareto frontier of accuracy and speed among the 25 decision models we tested,” the company said in a blog post. System 1 refers to the fast, intuitive mode of human thinking, as opposed to System 2, which involves slower and more deliberate reasoning. Sarvam said the model is intended for enterprise workflows that involve a sequence of decisions, such as intent routing, customer support, model selection and document intelligence. Prism recorded an average score of 71.8 across the Jev Decision Index, Sarvam’s recreation of the Artificial Analysis Decision Index, and an internal Indian-language benchmark. It scored 67 on the Jev Decision Index, 65.9 on the Artificial Analysis benchmark and 82.5 on the Indian-language benchmark. Sarvam said Prism is trained to provide calibrated confidence scores, allowing enterprises to determine when a model’s output can be used to automate a decision and when human intervention is required. When Prism was at least 90% confident in its answers, its error rate was 2.2% for English questions and 4.4% for Indian-language questions. The company also tested the model against changes in the order of answer options. Across 2,000 questions, Prism’s answers remained unchanged when options were shuffled after the model arranged them in a fixed order before scoring. “Prism makes fewer errors than its confidence scores predict, across every threshold we tested from 50% to 95%, in English and Indian languages,” the company said. Sarvam also tested Prism on agent trace evaluations and cybersecurity tasks. The model achieved 86.4% accuracy in identifying whether an agent run required human review and 75% accuracy in determining whether a task had been completed successfully. On an internal cybersecurity benchmark comprising 5,517 questions across nine tasks, Prism recorded 89% accuracy. The benchmark covered phishing detection, jailbreak attempts and classification of attacks using MITRE ATT&CK frameworks. Sarvam said Prism can evaluate an entire agent trace in about half a second on a single GPU and process up to 1,31,072 tokens per question.

items.title: These college students launched a legal tech startup during finals week. Now, it's business first, school second.
items.summary: Raphael Lim and Jamison Teng started a legal tech company in college. Raphael Lim Raphael Lim and Jamison Teng often juggle their legal tech startup with studies during finals. They've had to sacrifice social life, grades, and Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu training to build up Jam & Raph. But it's given them an opportunity to test a startup in a place where failure is not the end of the world. When Raphael Lim, 23, and Jamison Teng, 24, met in 2022, their time together was filled with Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu training and playing video games. But now, their hangouts look different as they work through the twists and turns of running a year-old legal technology startup . Lim and Teng are the cofounders of Jam & Raph, a startup that provides AI consultancy services to law firms. Juggling the demands of the startup alongside their law and computer science degrees at two of Singapore's top colleges hasn't been easy, often putting their studies on the back seat. How they got into legal tech Lim, a second-year computer science student at the National University of Singapore, and Teng, a final-year law student at the Singapore Management University, competed in a collegiate legal tech hackathon in 2024 and placed second. This gave them the idea to start a business in the legal tech space. "I saw that there was a lot of money being invested in the big firms like Harvey and Legora, so that's when I realized there was actually a market for this," Teng said. Harvey, one of the most prominent legal AI startups, has conducted several funding rounds over the past year and announced a valuation of $15.5 billion in September. Legora announced a $550 million Series D round in March, at a $5.55 billion valuation. Lim and Teng launched the company in November — finals season for both of them — with 2,500 Singapore dollars, or about $1,950, from SMU's entrepreneurship incubation program. They brought on 10 team members, all college students, and kickstarted Jam & Raph. Their product: Running workshops for law firms to teach lawyers how to use AI tools effectively and token-efficiently. They also started offering consultations to the firms, helping them build AI products tailored to their needs. Their workshops, which are two to three hours long, cost SG$2,000 to SG$3,000, and they charge SG$120 per hour for consultations. They poured a little of their savings into the venture — less than $2,000 combined — but operating expenses are low, mainly their $150 monthly Claude subscriptions and email domain fees. They say they've stuck all their revenue in their company bank account for now, not paying themselves anything. Putting out fires during finals week Despite studying in Singapore, a country that is infamous for its rigorous and competitive academic culture, both Teng and Lim said that working on the business always takes precedence over their studies. "My GPA took a total hit, but I think that's just the cost of doing a startup when you are in university, so that is to be expected," Lim said. Teng said he's seen his grades improve in classes that blend tech and law. His core law classes have taken a hit, but that hasn't phased him. "I think Singapore still places a lot of emphasis on academics, but the more we talk to people and clients outside Singapore, like Americans or Europeans, they care more about your story," he said. But problems always seem to arise at the most inconvenient times, they said, like clients calling them about product failures during their final weeks, when they have to study for multiple exams. It's also taken a toll on their social lives. "We've had clients sending emails saying, 'Hey, your product is down,' while we're having drinks with friends, and we have to immediately deal with it," Lim said. Lim said that he's missed out on a large part of the freshman college experience. "Everyone was out partying and joining clubs, meeting new people, and I would be cooped up in my room, coding," he said. He added that his ex-partner got angry at him when he didn't answer the phone all day while he was solving a technical issue for their product, and then had to complete schoolwork. The duo doesn't meet to practice Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu or play video games anymore, either, and their hangouts are all about work. It's better to fail in college For Teng, it was an opportunity to test out entrepreneurship in a safe space before entering the workforce. "It's okay to fail because if you fail as a student startup founder, I think it's pretty expected; there's no real heat that you can get in terms of responsibilities," he said, adding that people are a lot warmer toward student entrepreneurs. Lim said running a business is a good window to the world outside the classroom. "My peers will be doing a lot of academics, research theory, but I get to see how these theories actually apply in the real world," he said. Neither of them sees this as a replacement for a postgrad job hunt, though, with both saying that they want to get corporate work experience. "It was more of a 'good to have,' something we built for the love of the game to bring something to the world," Lim said. Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: From Fragmentation to Fusion: A Survey and Roadmap for Omnimodal Embeddings
items.summary: Embedding models underpin virtually every modern AI system, from search engines to recommendation systems. Despite shared mathematical foundations, research on embedding models remains fragmented by modality: the communities develop largely in isolation, seldom exchanging insights. We argue that this fragmentation obscures a deeper convergence. Driven by contrastive learning, Transformer architectures, and a granularity shift, embedding research across modalities is converging toward a common set of principles, even as modality-specific challenges remain underexplored. To reason across this convergence without conflating it, we propose a framework of three progressively harder capabilities: coverage, comparability, and compositionality. Three paths toward unification satisfy these in turn: transformation broadens coverage, alignment enables comparability, and joint embedding, the terminus we advocate, aims at compositionality. This position paper traces the resulting evolution, providing the first unified, cross-cutting treatment of omnimodal embedding research.

items.title: MEMENTO: Learning Context Management for Long Context Processing Agents
items.summary: LLM agents that operate over long inputs must perform context management: deciding what to retain in a fixed-size context window. A common approach is compaction, where the model replaces its history with a self-generated note. Yet off-the-shelf agentic models, including GPT-5.5 and GLM-5.3, often write ineffective notes, and reinforcement learning (RL) alone rarely discovers useful note-taking behavior. We present MEMENTO, a long-context agent built on Qwen3-8B and trained to manage its context through compaction. We first bootstrap note-taking by fine-tuning on synthetic trajectories annotated with notes generated in hindsight, then reinforce it with RL using a reward that combines answer correctness, note-quality heuristics, and confidence calibration. Although trained only to compact into a fresh window, MEMENTO extends at test time to strategies such as context folding and confidence-based backtracking. On book-level question answering across four benchmarks, with books of up to 2.5M tokens, MEMENTO raises Qwen3-8B's accuracy from 36.9% to 67.8% while never holding more than 20K tokens in context. It outperforms GPT-5.5 agent in the same harness (13.1%) and full book context (56.7%) at less than 1/50 the cost. It also nearly matches a ~100x larger GLM-5.3 agent (69.3%) at 1/9 the cost, and comes within 6.4 points of GLM-5.3 full context at 1/26 the cost.

items.title: Cross-Lingual Persona Effects in LLM Negotiation
items.summary: Tell an LLM negotiator to be "headstrong" and it should hold firm on price, but does that instruction retain the same behavior in every language? To test this, we use identical buyer and seller instances of Gemini 3.6 Flash to negotiate the same 12 CraigslistBargain scenarios in English and Korean. The pilot-scale 2 x 2 x 3 design crosses interaction language, seller urgency (none or strong), and buyer persona (cooperative, neutral, or headstrong), yielding 432 attempted negotiations. We call this property cross-lingual social-policy fidelity: whether a prompt-defined social policy produces the same behavioral effect regardless of interaction language. It often does not. Korean negotiations reached agreement far more often than English (77.3% vs. 52.5%, a 24.8-point gap, Holm-adjusted p = .0039), but only for neutral and headstrong buyers; cooperative buyers were already near-ceiling in both languages. Buyers' opening offers barely differed by language; the gap instead emerged later, through larger seller concessions and a smaller final gap in Korean, and agreed prices were also lower in Korean. Repeating the full design with Qwen3.7 Flash as both agents gives directional support: agreement was again higher in Korean (+13.9 points vs. Gemini's +24.8, with an interval whose lower bound is near zero), and sellers again conceded more. Pragmatic analysis reveals why: while both languages frequently featured face-threatening acts like rejections and counter-offers, Korean dialogue softened these threats with substantially more politeness mitigation, especially among sellers (11.7% vs. 3.6%). These results show that such a policy can produce different simulated negotiation behavior, not just different wording, when only the interaction language changes.

items.title: GAVAGAI: Referential Alignment for Infant-Scale Vision-Language Models via Balanced Optimal Transport
items.summary: A child learns which words name which things from roughly 100 million words of input. Vision-language models trained at a comparable scale bind words to referents far less reliably, and we argue that part of the gap is structural: the usual next-token captioning objective has no variable standing for "this word refers to that region," so training applies no direct pressure to ground words. We add such a variable by treating each scene as a small assignment problem between the content words heard and the regions seen, solved as entropic optimal transport under two constraints. First, a word may be assigned to a special NOTHING column instead of any region, which matters because most content words in caregiver speech do not name anything visible. Second, no region may receive more than a bounded share of the assignment mass, a capacity constraint that encodes mutual exclusivity. The alignment step costs about eight Sinkhorn iterations, small next to the vision encoder. In controlled simulation, the naive version of the idea, a row-wise softmax that forces every word onto some region, collapses to 0.000 word-to-picture accuracy under realistic non-reference rates, below the 0.058 of captioning alone, while our two constraints reach 0.075 in that regime and 0.700 on clean input. A one-parameter version of the model reproduces adult cross-situational learning accuracy across three ambiguity conditions (RMSE 0.024). On the SAYCam infant video corpus, adding the alignment loss to a next-token captioning model raises word-to-picture accuracy from 32.4% to 48.7% and localization IoU from 0.18 to 0.38. A contrastive model trained on the same child's data remains stronger on its own benchmark, so our claim is that the loss improves a captioning objective under high non-reference rates, not that it sets a new best.

items.title: Queering the Audits: Community-Based Auditing of AI Harms to Queer Communities
items.summary: AI systems embed majority-group defaults into training data, evaluation metrics, and category definitions, producing documented harms for queer communities including erasure, misclassification, and discrimination. Standard technical audits often rely on aggregate measures and cannot detect harms that be come visible only through the lived experience of affected communities. We conducted a participatory auditing workshop at EurIPS 2025 where 16 queer community members audited four case studies using the 4Cs harm taxonomy (Content, Conduct, Contact, Contract) applied across the AI lifecycle. Participants used structured worksheets and plenary synthesis to classify harms and trace them to their origins in the development pipeline. Across all four cases, participants traced harms to problem definition and data collection, and they identified contractual structures that extract value from vulnerable populations while providing minimal recourse. These findings illustrate that community-informed auditing surfaces concrete, identity-specific harms that aggregate evaluation methods risk overlooking.

items.title: Cross-Prompt Reuse of Entity-Replacement Responses
items.summary: With model weights fixed, we measure how much of an entity-replacement response transfers between English factual questions, beyond whether answers change. We add the hidden-state change from two source questions to a target question about the same entity, comparing the predicted log-probability shift between two relations' published answers, given known answer prefixes, with the measured one. Hidden reuse injects the aligned change at 50% depth before the target's remaining layers; direct reuse adds source output-score changes. With other-relation sources, hidden reuse removes 45% and 49% of no-change error on 0.5-1B Qwen and Llama. Gemma-2-2B removes 22% and passes one of three comparisons in plain text without its default beginning-of-sequence (BOS) token. A later protocol restoring it yields 58-68%, passing every comparison on three cohorts. Larger checkpoints, chat format and new entities show replication and format- or cohort-dependent failures. On small plain-format checkpoints, other-relation hidden reuse mainly reproduces the shift both relations' questions share, without reliably lowering relation-selective error. With target-relation sources, hidden reuse's post hoc advantage over direct reuse is 0.2-0.9 nats outside chat format, unconfirmed and not replacement-specific. The same relation-neutral change at both questions' entity tokens lowers relation-selective error more than random or other-replacement changes, indicating receiving-question dependence.

items.title: Humanized but Still True? Auditing Facts and Detection in AI-Text Humanizers
items.summary: AI "humanizers" rewrite machine-generated text so that detectors classify it as human-written. Public leaderboards score evasion and embedding similarity, but not whether checkable details survive. We check whether numbers, dates, person and organization names, and quoted spans survive each rewrite, using a rule-based checker validated by two AI annotators (precision 0.84-1.00, recall 0.93-0.95; no human annotation). In the October 2026 cycle of a public humanizer leaderboard, all 11 commercial tools changed or dropped at least one of these units in 35-65% of the documents that contained one. Most changes were to quoted spans; counting numbers and names alone, 10 of the 11 tools still altered at least one in 20% or more of the documents. The September 2026 cycle was similar (19-50%). An open 12B humanizer kept at least 97% of numbers and names in fact-dense U.S. federal agency text, but reworded 67-78% of the quoted spans, against its own prompt. Unit retention and detector evasion were not clearly related across tools (Spearman rho = -0.46, 95% CI -0.65 to 0.08), and the open model's four released files (two of them quantization-aware low-bit files) did not show the pre-registered monotone trade-off. On federal texts with matched human, AI-styled and humanized versions, a general-purpose decision model, Jev, asked a single zero-shot question, separated human originals from humanized rewrites with AUROC 0.864 (0.827-0.902), 0.18-0.22 higher than Binoculars, Fast-DetectGPT and the adversarially trained RADAR, while calling 24% of the human originals AI at a 0.5 threshold. On the AI-styled rewrites by 2026 models, both perplexity-based detectors scored below chance (AUROC 0.37 and 0.39), also with line breaks removed. Hypotheses, data rules and analyses were frozen before the main runs; two earlier data contacts are disclosed. We release the checker and the per-item results.

items.title: Circuit Oracle: Automating Attribution Graph Analysis via Natural-Language Queries
items.summary: Attribution graphs, an emerging tool in mechanistic interpretability, use transcoders to decompose language model computations into sparse interpretable features connected by causal edges. However, turning a graph into a safety-relevant insight requires hours of manual analysis by experts. We introduce Circuit Oracle, an off-the-shelf LLM equipped with a multi-agent harness and task-specific authored skills, which answers natural-language questions about a target model by reading the attribution graph through tool calls. We evaluate it on three safety-relevant proxy tasks: detecting spurious features in probe circuits, eliciting hidden knowledge from taboo-finetuned models, and suppression jailbreaking via feature-level interventions. Beyond task scores, the oracle produces pruned subgraphs and context-specific feature explanations that we assess qualitatively. Results are mixed. On spurious-feature detection, Circuit Oracle reaches 78.2 $\pm$ 2.4% accuracy, outperforming single-layer feature-ranking baselines. On secret elicitation, trained self-explainers like Activation Oracles remain the stronger baseline. On refusal suppression over 50 prompts, its single committed intervention is slightly below a diff-in-means baseline, and only exceeds it when allowed the best of five attempts. Results are stable across five runs and across model choices for the agents. We also release the pruned subgraphs and context-specific feature readings that revise existing global labels, and invite future work to develop evaluations that can measure their usefulness directly.

items.title: Fidelity Collapses with Table Size, Not Turn Count: Delivery Architecture in a Deployed Tool-Using Agent
items.summary: When a multi-turn agent delivers a tool's structured records into the model's context and re-emits them each turn, every turn can corrupt data the tool computed correctly. We measure this in a production award-travel agent: two architectures over identical frozen payloads, lineage-matched prompts and sampling, differing only in delivery architecture. SYNTHESIS feeds full record sets into the planner's context and answers follow-ups in-head; BYPASS, the deployed system, keeps records in session state, translates follow-ups into arguments for a deterministic filter, and delivers rows over a typed side channel. Across 24 dialogues (339 scored turns per condition), BYPASS scores 92.3% of turns fully correct, SYNTHESIS 45.7% (paired gap +46.6pp [+35.7, +57.1]). Varying delivered-table size by capture date, SYNTHESIS collapses from near-perfect at 10 rows or fewer to 8% or less beyond about 74 rows. On a content-controlled prefix ladder the collapse threshold orders by model capability, from under 10 rows (GPT-4o-mini) to about 198 or more (Gemini 2.5 Pro), while BYPASS stays size-flat for all four models. The collapse is expensive: beyond 100 rows, where almost no SYNTHESIS answer is correct, each correct one costs roughly 200x BYPASS's flat \$0.012. Practitioners converged on typed side-channel delivery for rendering, not correctness; we show it was, unknowingly, also a correctness decision.

items.title: From Lookups to Lessons: Turning Retrieved Knowledge into Parametric Memory
items.summary: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) helps large language models (LLMs) answer factual questions beyond their training data, but it adds storage and inference costs. Distilling previously retrieved information into parametric memories enables reuse without online retrieval. However, training the memory to mimic a retriever rewards accurate independent predictions, which do not necessarily improve the final output quality when combined with the LLM's existing predictions. To address this, we introduce ResMem, in which the LLM reads retrieved text offline to generate teacher targets. This design avoids storing massive token representations, unlike existing parametric memory approaches such as MLP Memory, which relies on k-nearest neighbor (kNN) datastores. Furthermore, by using the LLM as an offline teacher that reads privileged retrieved evidence alongside the input, we train a parametric memory to learn an additive logit residual. This residual aligns the predictions of a student sharing the same backbone with the teacher distribution, while self-distillation updates remain confined to the parametric memory. On a Wikipedia subset, ResMem reduces the storage retained for teacher construction by 94.7% compared with the evaluated kNN pipeline. Across five question answering datasets, ResMem raises mean token F1 from 32.83% for the frozen LLM to 34.48%. It also breaks 21% fewer of the LLM's correct answers than a kNN-trained memory. These findings validate our motivation of treating retrieval as a learning resource, with parametric memory shaped by how retrieved knowledge is used to inform the model's future predictions. Code and model weights are available at https://github.com/SSRand/From-Lookups-to-Lessons and https://huggingface.co/RandHan/ResMem-Mistral-7B-v0.3.

items.title: Steering Readerly Dynamics: Trajectory-Guided Story Generation with Large Language Models
items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to generate stories, but these stories struggle to reproduce engaging readerly dynamics, the evolving reader responses that shape narrative experience. To address this challenge, we propose a framework that learns readerly dynamics from high-quality human-written stories and uses them to guide story generation. Instead of directly modeling high-dimensional story content, we train a small LLM to predict future reader responses as low-dimensional trajectories. We then leverage the strong instruction-following capability of a larger, off-the-shelf writer LLM to generate story segments that follow these predicted trajectories within a given story setting. Our framework improves trajectory-based fidelity to human-written stories by 12%-35% while largely preserving story coherence.

items.title: Spotting the Artificial: Dialogic Humor Improvisation in Humans and LLMs
items.summary: We propose a methodology for investigating the differences between natural and synthetic language in a challenging setting: humorous improvisational dialogue. Our experimental setting compares human-produced comedy improvisations with the dialogues generated by LLMs in a multi-agent environment that we designed. The analysis combines automated linguistic measures with manual annotation grounded in Systemic Functional Linguistics (SFL). The results show that, although LLMs can create coherent and creative scenes, they often fail to reproduce key characteristics of spontaneous spoken interaction. In addition, LLM-generated interactions display a strong tendency toward politeness and positive evaluations, contrasting with the broader range of attitudes found in human humorous improvisation. Our evidence highlights both the strengths and limitations of current LLMs in modeling dialogic humor and demonstrate the value of integrating linguistic theory with NLP methods for the analysis of machine-generated language

items.title: AStockArena: Beyond Returns, Can We Entrust Real Capital to the Decisions of Financial Agents?
items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in dynamic financial trading, yet real-time trading benchmarks mainly evaluate agents by cumulative returns and risk-adjusted performance. Such outcome metrics cannot show whether trades are faithfully reported, supported by available evidence, and consistent with account states. We introduce AStockArena, a real-time decision-auditing benchmark for continuous trading in China's A-share market. Under shared market conditions and execution constraints, we evaluate 13 open- and closed-source models over 3,198 sequential decisions. AStockArena reconstructsthe actions actually posted to accounts by aligning reports, trade requests, execution responses, and account states, and audits them with eight checks spanning execution traceability (O), evidence sufficiency (RK), and financial meta-awareness (B), combining record verification with consensus expert annotation. Of 1,070 trading points, 72.99% exhibit at least one audit gap; model-level rates range from52.2% to 91.2%, with evidence gaps most prevalent. Historical trade-filtering replay further shows thatportfolio outcomes are sensitive to these flagged trades. Decision-process auditing thus offers a verifiable complement to return-based evaluation of financial agents.

items.title: Dual-Axis Policy Entailment: A Benchmark for Policy-Change Reasoning
items.summary: Whether a policy shifts domains and, by extension, continues, broadens, narrows, or reverses previous policy is of paramount importance to the study of public policy. We propose Dual-Axis Policy Entailment (DAPE), which evaluates an ordered pair of policy directives on both dimensions at once: a binary judgment determines whether the two directives govern the same policy domain, and a five-way judgment determines whether the later directive continues, broadens, narrows, or reverses the earlier policy, or governs a different domain altogether. Read together, the two judgments form one five-category label, our primary metric. The two-axis design captures two central dimensions of policy change without conflating errors on either dimension into a generic "irrelevant" label, and it makes annotation more rigorous: a coder cannot dismiss a difficult pair as domain-irrelevant without an explicit, checkable decision. We introduce an expert-annotated benchmark of 1,000 ordered directive pairs drawn from a large corpus of Chinese government policy, together with an annotation-calibration protocol (an adjudication packet with pre/post agreement measurement) that we contribute as a methodological artifact. Fourteen open-weight models and four frontier API flagships fail the task zero-shot: even the best frontier flagship's chance-corrected agreement with expert labels is far below the human ceiling (Cohen's $\kappa \approx 0.29$ vs. $0.53$). A fine-tuned open-weight model (LoRA SFT of Qwen3-14B, five-fold cross-validation) closes this gap, reaching the coder-mutual human ceiling ($\kappa = 0.524$ vs. $0.527$). Finally, we apply our method to China's AI policy (1980-2024) and map the direction of policy change across eras.

items.title: Distinguishing among reasoning levels of GPT 5.5 Pro via a grammar lens benchmark
items.summary: Does the level of test-time processing effort affect a language model's computational capability? A formal grammar-lens benchmark method, derived from the theory of computation, generates novel data at specified levels, each successively more computationally powerful than the levels below. Using this data, we tested GPT-5.5, and GPT-5.5-Pro-Medium, -High, and -XHigh, showing incrementally increased acceptance of test data: 16, 40, 43, and 52\%, respectively, illustrating the benchmark's ability to discern fine-grained differences among models' added test-time reasoning levels. Additionally, as test-time compute effort increases, model responses diverge from human responses to the same data. This increasing disagreement may turn out to be broadly characteristic of more capable language models, introducing the potential of a general capability-versus-alignment conflict.

items.title: From Apparent Search Gains to Selection Failures: Auditing Test-Time Inference in Structured Workflow Planning
items.summary: Test-time search can improve structured planning, but when methods differ in prompts, post-processing, and selection, it is unclear what an observed gain should be attributed to. We study this question on DisasterBench, where models compose typed multi-tool workflows, by decomposing inference into three observable stages: whether a correct workflow is discovered, whether it survives structural validation, and whether it is finally selected. Comparing independent sampling, a nominal tree-search configuration, and multi-operator search under controlled inference budgets on two model families, we find that (i) the nominal tree-search configuration realizes non-adaptive complete-workflow sampling, and independent sampling with its expansion prompt reproduces its candidate discovery without constructing a tree; (ii) structural validation never removes the last correct workflow in our evaluated candidate pools, whereas majority voting leaves a discovered correct workflow unselected on 10-19% of tasks per pool, with an audit confirming substantive tool-choice or information-flow errors in 57 of 60 examined cases; and (iii) a tool-specification-aware verifier recovers some of these losses but overturns more correct decisions than it fixes. Our results motivate auditing realized rather than nominal inference pipelines, and reporting discovery, validity, and selection separately.

items.title: Saidzoda-Tajik-E5-Large: Fine-Tuning a 560M Embedder for Tajik Retrieval
items.summary: Finding the passage that answers a question is the first step of most practical systems built on documents, and for Tajik we found no openly described model for it. We present Saidzoda-Tajik-E5-Large, a Tajik text embedder built from multilingual-e5-large-instruct (560M parameters). We asked our own Tajik language model to write questions for passages from Tajik laws, tax documents, Wikipedia and web text, and trained on 235,140 question and passage pairs for one epoch, with hard negatives chosen by another embedder and English and Russian pairs mixed in so the model would not forget those languages. On laws the model had never seen, the right passage is among the top ten results for 93.6% of questions, up from 80.2%; on tax documents, 94.5% against 82.6%. On Belebele, the one test we have that was written by people, the gain is smaller and not confirmed (92.2% to 95.2%, with touching intervals), and Russian and English do not change. On law and tax questions written in the same style as its training questions, it is tied with Giga-Embeddings-3B, a model five times its size; on Belebele the 3B and 8B models score slightly higher, and only after we fine-tuned them on our data are they clearly ahead. We also report what failed: training in bfloat16 broke the model, and replacing Tajik letters with similar Russian ones did not help. Our law, tax and Wikipedia test questions come from the same model that wrote the training questions, so we treat those scores as an upper limit until questions written by Tajik speakers are available.

items.title: Multi-Estimate Elicitation Does Not Uniformly Debias Language Model Judgments
items.summary: Does eliciting five weighted estimates within a single response change how a language model responds to information? Across anchoring, hindsight, base-rate, conjunction, and status-quo/default tasks, we compare direct numerical answers with a multi-estimate response format, contrasting source framings, explicitly random cues, and probability-consistency constraints. We evaluate three completed configurations--gpt-6.1-sol, claude-sonnet-5.5, and Qwen3-8B (reasoning disabled, analyzed descriptively). In the first two configurations, direct elicitation yielded near-zero irrelevant-anchor indices and status-quo effects, while remaining responsive to informative sources and informed advice. Of 23 preregistered confirmatory tests, six rejected after Holm adjustment; however, all six absolute point estimates fell below their prespecified smallest effect sizes of interest without establishing equivalence. Moreover, while separate versus joint elicitation shifted conjunction judgments, interpretation is constrained by between-call noise. Ultimately, multi-estimate elicitation failed to produce uniform debiasing or response attenuation across tasks and models, though post hoc correlations between candidate spread and anchoring error motivate independent predictive validation. Materials: https://github.com/asj252/llm-judgment-studies

items.title: Enhancing Language Model Reasoning with Structured Multi-Level Modeling
items.summary: Inference-time scaling enhances a model's reasoning by extending its chain-of-thought (CoT). However, existing approaches typically rely on a single policy trained with outcome-reward reinforcement learning (RL), which often suffers from long-horizon plan failures where the implicit plan drifts from valid strategies, especially for small LMs with limited capacity. To address this, we propose Multi-Level Reasoning (MLR), which reformulates long-CoT generation as a two-level stochastic process. A high-level planner generates structured step descriptors specifying both the reasoning mode and the semantic subgoal. The low-level executor then produces detailed reasoning conditioned on these descriptors, forming an alternating plan--execute loop. To maintain scalability, we adopt a minimal design where the base model serves as the low-level policy and a lightweight LoRA module implements the high-level policy. For training, we observe that outcome-reward RL provides sparse and delayed feedback for long trajectories (e.g., several thousand tokens), hindering credit assignment. We therefore introduce iterative Step-DPO, a process-level preference optimization scheme that leverages Twisted Sequential Monte Carlo (TSMC) to provide scalable stepwise supervision. This yields more effective training, improved stability, and higher accuracy. Extensive experiments on challenging math, science, and logical reasoning benchmarks show that, under the same reduced data budget (10% SFT and 5% preference relative to the DeepSeek-R1 distillation setup), MLR outperforms both SFT-based distillation and strong RL/preference-optimization baselines across multiple base models and tasks. Moreover, MLR exhibits slower performance degradation on long-horizon reasoning, demonstrating stronger robustness under extended CoT generation.

items.title: ElectroChemLLM: A Multimodal LLM Pipeline for High-Fidelity Electrochemical Informatics
items.summary: Electrochemistry is central to solving many modern-day challenges, including energy storage systems for a sustainable future, and its advancement relies heavily on the data from past findings. Existing automated pipelines are limited by text-only architectures, context fragmentation, and numerical hallucinations - collectively preventing accurate, large-scale curation of property databases. We introduce ElectrochemLLM, a multimodal information extraction pipeline that jointly identifies structured electrochemical records encompassing electrolyte compositions, electrode materials, cell configurations, and their measured physicochemical properties from unstructured scientific PDFs at scale. By combining hybrid document parsing with vision-capable LLM orchestration, the pipeline extracts verifiable, structured data across text, tables, and figures. Evaluated on the battery-electrolyte subset of our manually annotated benchmark of 232 papers, ElectrochemLLM achieves an F-1 score of 0.97, and has been applied to curate ElectroChemDB, a structured database spanning 15,000 electrochemical research articles. We demonstrate the utility of this resource by training machine learning models for electrolyte property prediction, illustrating a complete pathway from unstructured literature to predictive materials discovery.

items.title: Audit at the Precision You Deploy: Quantization Reshapes a Subliminally Learned Preference
items.summary: Subliminal learning allows AI models to inherit hidden preferences from seemingly unrelated training data, such as number sequences. Safety audits may evaluate models at standard 16-bit precision, while deployments may use compressed, quantized weights. We ask whether quantization changes the expression of a subliminal preference and what drives any resulting change. To investigate, we implant a "favourite animal: panda" preference into Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct. We define its net strength as the difference in mean panda-answer probability between subliminal models and neutrally trained controls under the same quantization setting. Applying this metric across different compression levels reveals a stark contrast. While behaviour remains stable at 8 bits, 4-bit quantization triggers severe, opposing shifts depending on the quantizer. Half-Quadratic Quantization (HQQ) amplifies the preference, raising the subliminally trained model's panda probability from roughly 55% at 16 bits to 64% at 4 bits, while the controls stay near 17%. This raises the trait's net strength ~1.3 times its 16-bit value. In contrast, NormalFloat (NF4) at 4-bit suppresses it, shrinking the net strength to just ~0.3 times its 16-bit value, despite producing rounding errors of the same size to within 4%. We examine the structure of the rounding errors and find that their arrangement drives the divergence. Randomly shuffling HQQ's errors within each quantization group, without changing their magnitude, shifts the trait's net strength between 0.2 and 1.6 times its 16-bit value. Despite these opposing shifts, the underlying fine-tuning signal remains largely intact. Because a model's internal state and outward behaviour diverge so unpredictably under compression, a 16-bit audit cannot reliably bound real-world risks. Safety evaluations must test the exact quantized weights intended for deployment.

items.title: Precedent Labels and Facts Shift LLM Approval Decisions in Opposite Directions
items.summary: When a language model decides refund or claim requests under written policies, the system can show it similar past cases. Each past case has two parts: its facts and the decision recorded for it. We separate the two. A model sees a policy, a request and three past cases, and we change either the recorded decisions or the facts, keeping the request fixed. We select requests that are close calls: deciding without past cases, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash approved each in some of four tries and denied it in others. When the past cases are near-copies of the request (its facts with a few details changed), switching their recorded decisions from DENY to APPROVE raises approval by about 30 to 55 percentage points in DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, GPT-5.6 Luna and Claude Haiku 5.5 on policies written for the study, and DeepSeek and Luna show the same on nine public policies paraphrased from real ones. The facts push the other way: shown without their recorded decisions, past cases whose facts support approval make these two models approve less often than past cases whose facts support denial. One reading is that the request looks weaker next to them. This push is not just a correction toward the right answer: in an additional DeepSeek analysis, it was of similar estimated size on requests that human annotators judged approvable and on those they judged deniable. In a separate DeepSeek run on the public policies, when the past cases are near-copies of a different request, switching their decisions moves approval by 9 points instead of 43, while facts that support approval still lower it by 22 points against facts that support denial. Systems that retrieve past decisions should test the two parts separately.

items.title: Constructing Budgeted KGW Evasion through Token-Event Evidence Replacement
items.summary: KGW watermarks bias sampling to accumulate keyed detection evidence. We construct budgeted evasion through token-event evidence replacement using ordinary phrase rewrites. Our construction jointly selects compositions of LLM-proposed alternatives from an independent model and measures global token-edit distance on complete outputs. At the largest attainable cost within the budget, exact coverage search maximizes removal of original scored token pairs. It uses a known tokenizer without the key, detector feedback or queries to the watermarked model. Exact accounting separates source evidence removed, evidence created and length effects, with initial strength setting the required reduction. Separate signed-event analysis found that mean suppression arose mainly from removing watermark-enriched source events. In controlled, occurrence-counted, one-token-context KGW tests on short passages, 39 of 82 qualified, initially detected sources yielded rewrites with terminal detector score Z < 4 that passed blinded source-relative model review, at a mean actual token-edit cost of 16.0% under a 20% allowance. To examine whether this initial requirement can be inferred, a separate historical 95-passage study estimated initial detector score Z0 from generation traces with correlation 0.793 and an in-sample association beyond length. This aggregate information did not establish improved allocation, and the separate no-trace stopping test did not reliably exploit cheaper reviewed crossings in the candidate bank. Comparisons did not establish an advantage over simpler selection and ordinary constrained rewriting. The construction makes budgeted evidence replacement executable while exposing limits in signed reduction and recognition of sufficient editing.

Abstract: KGW watermarks bias sampling to accumulate keyed detection evidence. We construct budgeted evasion through token-event evidence replacement using ordinary phrase rewrites. Our construction jointly selects compositions of LLM-proposed alternatives from an independent model and measures global token-edit distance on complete outputs. At the largest attainable cost within the budget, exact coverage search maximizes removal of original scored token pairs. It uses a known tokenizer without the key, detector feedback or queries to the watermarked model. Exact accounting separates source evidence removed, evidence created and length effects, with initial strength setting the required reduction. Separate signed-event analysis found that mean suppression arose mainly from removing watermark-enriched source events. In controlled, occurrence-counted, one-token-context KGW tests on short passages, 39 of 82 qualified, initially detected sources yielded rewrites with terminal detector score Z < 4 that passed blinded source-relative model review, at a mean actual token-edit cost of 16.0% under a 20% allowance. To examine whether this initial requirement can be inferred, a separate historical 95-passage study estimated initial detector score Z0 from generation traces with correlation 0.793 and an in-sample association beyond length. This aggregate information did not establish improved allocation, and the separate no-trace stopping test did not reliably exploit cheaper reviewed crossings in the candidate bank. Comparisons did not establish an advantage over simpler selection and ordinary constrained rewriting. The construction makes budgeted evidence replacement executable while exposing limits in signed reduction and recognition of sufficient editing.
