items.title: EffComp: Efficient Prompt Compression via Hybrid Reinforcement & Supervised Learning
items.summary: Prompt compression is aimed at reducing input prompt lengths to enable cheaper, faster, and potentially higher-quality LLM predictions. However, existing prompt compression methods are often limited by modest compression gains, a risk of hallucination, and/or high compression latency. We propose EffComp, an Efficient prompt Compression framework for RAG-based question answering (QA). EffComp employs BERT-style document reranker and sentence selector models to allow fast extractive prompt compression at the sentence level. Its extractive nature prevents hallucinations in the compressed prompts. Additionally, the training process using a hybrid reinforcement and supervised learning approach is designed to optimize the compression ratio while preserving LLM accuracy. Experiments on various QA datasets demonstrate that EffComp outperforms state-of-the-art prompt compression methods achieving the best trade-off between compression ratio and accuracy with minimal latency. This makes it practical for real-world applications.

items.title: PGuard: A Native, Streaming, and Plug-in Guardrail for Multimodal Large Language Models
items.summary: As streaming generation becomes the dominant serving paradigm for both text-only and multimodal large language models, ensuring safety throughout the generation process has become a critical challenge. We introduce PGuard, a native, streaming, and plug-in guardrail that transforms safety monitoring from an external serving dependency into an integrated capability of the backbone model. PGuard directly leverages the backbone's intermediate representations for token-level safety detection, without altering its original inference pathway or generation behavior. Specifically, dynamic layer gating selectively aggregates residual-stream representations across layers to extract safety-relevant signals during both prefill and autoregressive decoding. To balance detection accuracy and computational efficiency, PGuard supports multiple representation-modeling architectures, including a lightweight stateless variant and sequence-aware variants built on multi-scale causal EMA-attention and GRU-based recurrent modules. Its design also accounts for the execution characteristics of LLM serving frameworks, such as SGLang, optimizing computation and data access to minimize additional runtime and synchronization overhead. As a result, PGuard incurs only 0.82-2.26% end-to-end overhead on the hundred-billion-parameter backbone Qwen3.5-122B-A10B served by SGLang. Extensive evaluations across more than 30 benchmarks spanning text and multimodal safety, jailbreaks, cyber and CBRN risks, multilingual scenarios, and real-world traffic demonstrate state-of-the-art performance among native guardrails. On text queries with Qwen3.5-9B, PGuard achieves an average F1 score of 0.836, approaching dedicated external guardrails, while supporting deployment-time configuration of category-specific thresholds and enforcement actions.

items.title: TRIO: Task Refinement with Individual Optimization for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
items.summary: This paper studies retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), which leverages external knowledge to improve the performance of language models. Despite the remarkable progress, current RAG approaches are still far from satisfactory due to inadequate retrieval and potential hallucinations. Towards this end, we propose a novel approach named Task Refinement with Individual Optimization (TRIO) for RAG. The core idea of our TRIO is to equip three well-designed agents with an iterative refinement paradigm by aligning their individual optimization objectives. Specifically, we first expand ambiguous queries with a query extension agent and quantify the reward based on the improved answer quality, which can be utilized to refine our agent for higher expansion efficiency. To enhance the retrieval quality, we include a unanimity voting to annotate the expanded query as insufficient or sufficient, and their generative outcomes are utilized as ground truth to optimize the judge agent. To further improve evidence utilization and answer accuracy, an answer agent is optimized with dynamic matching-based rewards with curriculum learning for final outputs. Extensive experiments across multiple benchmark datasets validate the effectiveness of the proposed TRIO in comparison with state-of-the-art approaches. Our code is available at https://github.com/yingtaoren/TRIO.

items.title: Window-Aware Scheduling for Health Messaging under Platform Delivery Constraints: Evidence from an AI-Powered WhatsApp Maternal and Infant Health Chatbot in Nigeria
items.summary: WhatsApp lets a business send free-form messages only within 24 hours of a user's last message; outside this customer service window, only pre-approved templates are delivered. Health chatbots inherit this rule, but its cost is rarely measured. We analyse 98,607 messages sent to 3,696 mothers by a WhatsApp maternal health chatbot in Nigeria, with a largely separate export as replication. No free-form message failed with the window open (0 of 35,500), and failure jumped by 93.0 percentage points (95% CI 87.0 to 99.1) at exactly 24 hours. Two flows produced 66.1% of failures, including an offer to speak with a medical professional that, as built, reached 0.3 in 100 mothers whose window had closed. We formalise window-aware scheduling as a decision problem with an action of known zero value. Model-based offline evaluation, with bounds for unconfirmed delivery, estimates that sending the offer as an approved template would reach 81.5 to 86.8 in 100 such mothers, against 16.6 for waiting and 11.6 for a reply prompt. In a calibrated simulation, tabular Q-learning converges to the same template rule and does not beat it in any of 13 stress tests, and opting out does not rise with message volume. The main gain comes from respecting the platform rule, and it needs no learning. All outcomes are deliveries, not health outcomes.

items.title: Omni-Life: Benchmarking Omnimodal Real-Time AI Assistants in People's Daily Lives
items.summary: Real-time omnimodal assistants are expected to support people in everyday life, but audiovisual understanding alone does not establish whether they can provide timely and appropriate help. We introduce Omni-Life, a benchmark grounded in real-world user needs, deployment scenarios, and device-dependent observations. It combines controlled video synthesis for hazardous situations and edge cases with annotated real-world videos under a shared temporal protocol. The benchmark contains 400 videos: 290 requiring assistance, with 555 required intervention events, and 110 requiring silence throughout to test whether models can withhold unnecessary responses when no assistance is needed. We evaluate twelve configurations featuring mainstream real-time omnimodal models, jointly assessing event coverage, response content, timing, and unwanted output. At most 4.48% of videos requiring assistance are handled completely correctly. To examine practical deployment strategies, we study task reminders and response-latency tolerance. Reminders can improve recall by 17.12 percentage points but add approximately 4.6 unwanted responses per minute of reference silence. Increasing latency tolerance by 10s improves recall by at most 5.95 percentage points. These results show that existing models remain insufficient to deliver reliable assistance in real-life applications, calling for tailored model optimization in instruction following, timely proactive intervention, and withholding responses when assistance is not needed.

items.title: Tug of Watts: A study on the Energy - Accuracy Trade-off of Large Language Models on Medical Question Answering Tasks
items.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used in medical question answering (QA) systems. While recent works aim at incrementally improving the downstream task accuracy, an empirical estimation of the models' energy consumption and the associated carbon footprints is often overlooked. In this study, we demonstrate how practitioners can estimate energy consumption and arrive at reliable emission estimates for medical QA tasks available in the OpenMedical-LLM leaderboard by investigating 13 LLMs from 3 model families ranging from 270M to 14B parameters. We discuss how one can critically interpret energy versus accuracy trade-offs for a set of models for a given task. With this work, we underline that reporting disjoint energy and accuracy metrics alone does not suffice for careful trade-off assessments, but it also demands systematic construction and interpretation of joint trade-off metrics. We envisage such studies aiding practitioners in adopting better and more efficient models for their task and helping them become active participants in building sustainable LLM pipelines.

With this work, we underline that reporting disjoint energy and accuracy metrics alone does not suffice for careful trade-off assessments, but it also demands systematic construction and interpretation of joint trade-off metrics. We envisage such studies aiding practitioners in adopting better and more efficient models for their task and helping them become active participants in building sustainable LLM pipelines.

items.title: Maswao: An automatically collected, prepared, and benchmarked dataset for the South African Sign language
items.summary: Recent advancements in sign language processing can be attributed to developments in both large-scale dataset collection and algorithmic complexity in areas such as pose estimation techniques, signal processing through Transformer models, and model optimization. However, only a handful of sign languages, such as the American, British, and German, from over 200 globally recognized sign languages, reap the benefits of such advancements, while the rest lag behind. In this study, we aim to address this technological disparity by proposing a framework for the automatic collection and preparation of sign language datasets, with very minimal human-labour intervention, using the South African Sign Language (SASL) as a testbed. Specifically, we automatically collect SASL video content using public resources such as news broadcasts. Additionally, we convert their accompanying audio streams into text using available Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) tools. Furthermore, we crop the sign language area in the videos and use gradient descent to locate valleys of non-motion to determine end-of-sentence points within long videos to create our weakly sentence-aligned parallel corpora -- the Maswao (Signs) dataset. Finally, we benchmark the weakly aligned dataset on the task of Sign-to-text Translation using Recurrent Neural Networks and Transformer models to compare their individual intricacies. Our results show that Transformer models proposed in the literature outperform recurrent baselines, with the best-performing Transformer achieving BLEU-1 to BLEU-4 scores of 13.78, 5.21, 2.52, and 1.54, respectively, as well as ChrF = 18.09 and ROUGE-L = 10.51. These results indicate that the task remains promising and warrants further investigations.

items.title: A State Change Is Local, Its Consequences Are Not: Dependency-Aware State Revision for Long-Term Agent Memory
items.summary: Long-lived agents rely on persistent memory of users, tasks and decisions, and this memory must stay consistent with a world that keeps changing. When an upstream fact changes, however, memory systems can revise the contradicted memory itself while the beliefs, plans and actions derived from it remain accepted, even though they have lost their support. We therefore formulate dependency-aware state revision, which asks not only what changed but also which dependent states should no longer be trusted. To address it, StateGraph maintains an evolving state dependency graph whose edges are recovered from interaction histories. Its core design is counterfactual verification: each candidate edge is tested by asking whether the dependent state would survive the loss of its premise, which separates support dependence from semantic relatedness, and revision then invalidates a dependent state only when a strict dependency fails and no independent support path survives. To test this design, we introduce StateChangeBench, a controlled benchmark of 50 author-constructed cases annotated with cascade depth, hard negatives and action consequences. On it, StateGraph's Impact-F1 margin over a CUPMem reimplementation is 6.9 percentage points at depth 1 and 26.0 at depth 3+. On public long-term memory benchmarks, its point estimates are comparable to or higher than those of the evaluated baselines on most datasets. These results provide initial evidence that explicit dependency tracking can improve selective memory revision under changing conditions.

items.title: PlagiaCorpus: A Bilingual, Adversarial, and Cross-Lingual Dataset for Forensic Plagiarism Detection
items.summary: PlagiaCorpus is a bilingual Arabic-English dataset for benchmarking plagiarism and text-reuse detection, including reuse produced by large language models (LLMs) and reuse across languages. It contains 198,643 text records: a source corpus of 34,885 passages drawn from English and Arabic Wikipedia and two openly licensed book collections, and 163,758 queries (147,381 for training and 16,377 for testing). The queries cover five reuse classes of increasing difficulty, namely verbatim copying, character-level obfuscation, same-language paraphrasing by two different LLMs, and English--Arabic translation with structural paraphrasing, together with a Safe class of non-reused passages. Every positive query is linked to its source passage, and the train/test split is grouped by source passage so that no passage contributes queries to both splits. The release was curated through language identification, removal of LLM generation artefacts, and exact and cross-lingual de-duplication. Technical validation reports per-class length statistics, automatic checks of the train/test split, and inter-annotator agreement on a manually rated sample. The dataset is distributed in JSON and Parquet formats under a CC BY-SA 4.0 license.

items.title: Distilling Literary Sentiment from LLM Annotations into an Ordinal BERT Model
items.summary: The scarcity of human-annotated literary corpora limits the development of domain-specific sentiment analysis models. This study investigates whether LLM-generated annotations can supervise smaller models for literary sentiment analysis. We fine-tune five BERT models using ordinal regression on 10,889 literary sentences annotated by Gemma 4 31B on a ten-point sentiment scale. The models are evaluated against 1,923 human-annotated sentences from Hemingway's "The Old Man and the Sea", alongside the teacher model and conventional baselines. BERT-large achieves a Kendall's $\tau$ of 0.589, approaching the teacher's 0.604. Although a constant-neutral predictor achieves the lowest overall mean absolute error (MAE), BERT-base outperforms the teacher on non-neutral sentences, achieving an MAE of 0.726 versus 1.116. These findings demonstrate the potential of LLM-generated supervision for developing smaller literary sentiment models, while highlighting the limitations of aggregate error metrics on predominantly neutral datasets.

items.title: Finding Errors Is Not Enough: Selective Model Escalation for Entity-Targeted Sentiment Analysis
items.summary: Improving a sentiment classifier with limited resources involves more than simply deciding how much data to collect or which model to train. A labelled collection may lack examples of an important class. Once trained, a classifier may benefit from another model even when that model is weaker on its own. We study these decisions in document-level Entity-Level Sentiment Analysis (ELSA), primarily using South Slavic news. We first compare acquisition orders as collections grow. We then use uncertainty to choose which predictions to revisit, how many to process, and whether an alternative encoder or local LLM can correct them. Finally, we select complete routing policies on development data for held-out evaluation. Minority-prioritised acquisition helps at some very small training sizes, but not consistently thereafter. On SentiCoref, an oracle correcting all errors in the least-confident 10% without harming correct predictions would add 9.14 Macro-F1 points; however the best evaluated action gains only 0.90. Encoder averaging helps on AspectBench and NewsMTSC but harms SentiCoref, where selective LLM assistance is more promising. Both development-selected policies route 30% of records to the encoder-assisted LLM, yielding observed gains of 1.02 points on SentiCoref (interval includes zero) and 1.71 on NewsMTSC, at substantially different inference costs.

items.title: VERS: Steering Reasoning Models by Editing Their Activation Explanations
items.summary: Reasoning language models write a chain of thought before they answer, and many checks in it do not change the final answer. Natural language autoencoders (NLAs) explain a model's activations in text and rebuild activations from text, and editing an explanation can steer a model at a single token. We study whether such edits can also steer how a model reasons. We build VERS (Verbalize, Edit, Reconstruct, Steer): it turns explanation edits at the doubt points of one reasoning trace into one fixed direction, and adds this direction at paragraph breaks. On the full GSM8K test, VERS cuts generated tokens by 45.8% at an accuracy change of -0.82 percentage points (pp); on MATH-500 it saves 31.3% at -3.05 pp. At half strength, its trade-off between tokens and accuracy lies between those of the published methods SEAL and DEER. With fitted affine maps and a strength tuned for each model, the direction transfers to larger Qwen3 models, up to 235B-A22B, and saves 30-35% of tokens. On competition problems, however, VERS loses 3-7 pp at every model size, and a fixed direction did not separate necessary checks from unneeded ones.

items.title: Unlocking Criminal Court Decisions: Flexible Information Extraction for Empirical Legal Research
items.summary: Criminal verdicts contain descriptions of criminal behavior that can support quantitative legal research, but structuring them requires attributes and extraction rules that cannot always be fully specified in advance. We present an LLM-based pipeline that builds a structured dataset through attribute exploration, text span extraction, and value normalization, guided by annotation instructions that legal experts can refine. We evaluate it on two traffic offenses: driving under the influence (DUI) and driving despite a ban (DDB). For DUI, revising the instructions was associated with higher extraction accuracy (from 52% to 70% of correctly extracted values) and higher agreement between human annotators. Repeated runs of the same model agreed with each other more than with the gold annotations, showing that consistent output is not necessarily correct, while disagreement between annotators and between models helped reveal unclear instructions. For DDB, where the instructions defined fixed categories and output formats, agreement was high for most attributes.

items.title: SAGE (Subjectivity-Aware Generation Estimator): A Linguistic Framework for AI-Generated Review Detection *
items.summary: We propose a simple, linguistically motivated approach to detecting AI-generated peer reviews based on the inherently human trait of subjectivity. We capture subjectivity at two levels: the semantic level of evaluative language and modality and the pragmatic level of speech acts. Using features derived from speech act annotations and model-predicted subjectivity scores, we train a lightweight classifier that achieves an AUROC of 0.9566 with only these linguistic features. Combining its output with the state-of-the-art detector Sem-Detect raises the TPR at 1% FPR of Sem-Detect on the APRDB benchmark from 0.874 to 0.985, outperforming the current state of the art. Our results show that linguistic features of subjectivity provide an explainable source of information for detecting AI-generated peer reviews and can be readily integrated into existing detection methods. The code and models are publicly available on GitHub (https://github.com/Arys02/generated\_ text\_detection\_hub) and Hugging Face (https://huggingface.co/Arys02), respectively.

items.title: An Experimental Study of Hybrid Retrieval, NLI and Open-source LLMs for Scientific Claim Verification
items.summary: Claim verification is the task of deciding whether a source text supports a claim, contradicts it, or lacks sufficient evidence. Natural Language Inference (NLI) models can judge whether a single sentence supports or contradicts a claim, but they struggle when the evidence is spread across several sentences. Conversely, Large Language Models (LLMs) can reason across sentences, but may draw conclusions the text does not support. In this experimental study, we test whether a conservative fusion rule, labeling a claim Support or Contradict only when both models agree and defaulting to Not Enough Evidence otherwise, combines their strengths. We construct a benchmark of 2,035 claims from SciFact and CliniFact (858 Support, 152 Contradict, 1,025 Not Enough Evidence). We retrieve the top five most relevant sentences per claim using a hybrid of semantic and lexical (BM25) retrieval, which slightly outperforms either method alone. These retrieved sentences are then provided to every verification model. We then compare a DeBERTa-v3-base-mnli-fever-anli NLI baseline against Llama 3.1 8B, Qwen3 8B, and Mistral 7B. Qwen3 achieves the highest Macro-F1 (0.7937), followed by Llama 3.1 (0.7204) and Mistral (0.6388), while the NLI baseline reaches only 0.3157. Contrary to our hypothesis, fusion degrades performance, dropping Macro-F1 to 0.7392, 0.6730, and 0.5991, respectively. To understand this decline, we analyze agreements, disagreements, and common error patterns between the NLI and LLM verifiers. Our error analysis shows that NLI and LLM disagreements often result in correct LLM predictions being overturned.

items.title: Meet Students Where They Are: Student-Prefix Teacher Adaptation for On-Policy Distillation
items.summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) mitigates the student's exposure bias by optimizing on student-generated trajectories. However, student-generated prefixes may contain reasoning errors or follow patterns unfamiliar to the teacher, undermining the reliability of its token-level supervision. This degradation becomes more pronounced as prefixes grow longer. To address this teacher-side distribution mismatch, we propose Student-Prefix Teacher Adaptation (SPTA), which adapts the teacher to the states on which it is queried during distillation. Specifically, before OPD starts, we collect student rollout prefixes with random lengths and continually train the teacher to continue from the prefixes using reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR). By treating each prefix as context and rewarding correct final answers, the teacher learns to recover from student-induced states rather than imitate the student's reasoning. Then, the adapted teacher is used for standard OPD, with no changes to the distillation objective. Experiments on mathematical reasoning benchmarks show that our SPTA improves average student performance over standard OPD and OPD with task-level RLVR-adapted teachers. These results highlight the importance of adapting teachers not only to solve problems independently, but also to provide reliable guidance on the states their students actually visit.

items.title: DepthGraft: Structural Regularization through Hierarchical Cross-Layer KV Reconstruction
items.summary: Scaling depth is a key route to stronger large language models, but Pre-LN architectures often suffer from depth-wise information dilution, limiting the effective use of deep layers. While cross-layer connectivity has proven effective at mitigating this problem, existing designs usually introduce additional computation or memory access. We revisit cross-layer KV sharing as an efficient form of such connectivity. Beyond cache compression, each KV reuse edge creates a direct gradient path from deep layers to source KV projections, turning KV sharing into an implicit structural regularizer for KV representation geometry. We provide a systematic analysis of this mechanism, showing that proper sharing topologies sharpen key retrieval directions while enriching the value content subspace, whereas existing adjacent or global-anchor designs do not fully exploit this effect. Motivated by this, we propose DepthGraft, a hierarchical KV-sharing architecture that reconstructs deep-layer KV from stride-aligned shallow-middle source pairs. DepthGraft distributes non-local gradient flow across source layers, while preserving prefill early completion and reducing KV cache by roughly one third. Experiments on dense and MoE models from 0.5B to 16B parameters show consistent downstream improvements under both GQA and MLA. Notably, on the 16B MoE model, DepthGraft achieves a 7.0% absolute improvement on MMLU-Pro, along with gains of 6.6% on CMMLU and 6.4% on C3. These results validate the potential of DepthGraft as a scalable design for large-scale pretraining. The project page is available at https://github.com/jianke0604/DepthGraft.

items.title: ACTOR: Action-Centered Temporal Organization for Literary Role-Playing Agents
items.summary: Large language agents for literary role-playing are typically modeled around dialogue generation, leaving characters' non-dialogue behaviors and their dynamic evolution over story time underrepresented. In this paper, we propose ACTOR (Action-Centered Temporal Organization for Literary Role-Playing Agents), an automated framework for constructing such behavior trajectories from raw novel texts. ACTOR extracts dialogue and persona-relevant non-dialogue behaviors, represents each behavior using a Thought-Action-Observation structure, and organizes behavior trajectories according to the internal temporal order of the story. We build a behavior dataset from 143 diverse literary works. For each source behavior, we generate counterfactual behaviors that are contextually plausible yet inconsistent with the character's persona. We find that existing models struggle to reliably infer character-consistent actions from historical behaviors and evolving character states. Using these behavior pairs, we train models with Regularized Preference Optimization (RPO), which augments DPO with a negative log-likelihood loss on the source behavior to jointly optimize behavior preference and generation. We further design a four-way next-behavior selection task to evaluate the model's ability to faithfully mimic character actions. Across 17,560 evaluation instances, the model trained on ACTOR's preference pairs achieves substantially improved accuracy. This result demonstrates that structured, temporally organized supervision enables models to leverage character profiles and prior behaviors to infer subsequent actions, greatly advancing literary role-playing beyond mere dialogue imitation. Code and data are available at https://github.com/SilentStar233/ACTOR.

ACTOR extracts dialogue and persona-relevant non-dialogue behaviors, represents each behavior using a Thought-Action-Observation structure, and organizes behavior trajectories according to the internal temporal order of the story. We build a behavior dataset from 143 diverse literary works. For each source behavior, we generate counterfactual behaviors that are contextually plausible yet inconsistent with the character's persona. We find that existing models struggle to reliably infer character-consistent actions from historical behaviors and evolving character states. Using these behavior pairs, we train models with Regularized Preference Optimization (RPO), which augments DPO with a negative log-likelihood loss on the source behavior to jointly optimize behavior preference and generation. We further design a four-way next-behavior selection task to evaluate the model's ability to faithfully mimic character actions. Across 17,560 evaluation instances, the model trained on ACTOR's preference pairs achieves substantially improved accuracy. This result demonstrates that structured, temporally organized supervision enables models to leverage character profiles and prior behaviors to infer subsequent actions, greatly advancing literary role-playing beyond mere dialogue imitation. Code and data are available at https://github.com/SilentStar233/ACTOR.

items.title: Written Once, Read Differently How Language Models Own Answers Steer Their Next Ones
items.summary: When a language model answers a yes/no question, that answer changes how it answers a different question about the same entity. We study this \emph{self-commitment} in 22 open-weight models from four families (0.5B--72B parameters), fixing the model's first answer and measuring the shift in its second across 3,600 question pairs about 120 entities. Each answer writes a \emph{commitment direction} into the residual stream. The similarity of two questions' directions predicts their coupling on held-out entities ($\rho = 0.43$--$0.85$), and ablating a single direction shared across topics leaves at most 17\% of the effect in every model. How this direction is read is far less stable: the reading circuit spreads across more attention heads as models grow, instruction tuning makes more questions read it in the opposite sense, and in one model changing only the system prompt reverses the circuit's sign. Ablating the direction while sparing the attention sink removes most of the coupling at under 1.3\% perplexity cost in 18 of 19 instruction-tuned models, though it shifts standalone answers in two. Without the sink spared, the direction's alignment with the leading principal component of ordinary text predicts which models pay a high cost. Written once, the commitment is read differently across scale, training and prompt.

items.title: Specificity Bias and the Wikipedia Paradox: An xAI Analysis of AI Text Detectors under Domain Shift
items.summary: The widespread adoption of Large Language Models (LLMs) demands reliable detection of human-authored versus synthetic text. However, current Transformer-based detectors often experience severe performance degradation during domain shifts and operate as opaque classifiers. This paper investigates the robustness and interpretability of fine-tuned Transformer models (DistilBERT, RoBERTa) by evaluating them against a custom out-of-distribution (OOD) dataset of hyper-local news synthesized via open-source LLMs (Llama 3, Mistral, Gemma). To analyze model decision boundaries, we apply a tripartite Explainable AI (xAI) framework using SHAP. Our analysis reveals three key phenomena: First, detectors often rely on a "Call-to-Action" syndrome inherent to instruction-tuned LLMs rather than generic machine text. Second, we observe a "Specificity Bias," where LLMs successfully bypass detection by hallucinating specific named entities and mimicking conversational imperfection. Finally, we illustrate the "Wikipedia Paradox," wherein formal, objective human writing is frequently misclassified as AI due to its low statistical burstiness. These findings demonstrate that purely statistical detection paradigms face systematic limitations in highly structured human domains, emphasizing the critical need for semantically-aware, interpretable detection architectures.

items.title: MultiInpaintCOCO: Fine-Grained Visual Understanding in Multiple Languages
items.summary: Previous research shows that vision-language (VL) models struggle to understand fine-grained image details and tend to focus on the overall layout. Moreover, any weakness in English tends to be further amplified in the multilingual setting. To study that, we extend InpaintCOCO, an English dataset focused on fine-grained visual details, to 13 typologically diverse languages across five language families, creating MultiInpaintCOCO - a new multilingual benchmark of 953 minimal-pair examples. We further test several state-of-the-art models in multilingual multimodal retrieval, considering both light VL CLIP-like encoders and large language models. Our results show that performance degrades substantially for lower-resource languages, with the strongest predictor being the data resources available for the languages rather than typological similarity to English. In cross-lingual retrieval, most models exhibit a systematic bias toward English: when given a correct caption in a non-English language and an incorrect one in English, models preferentially select the English caption. This bias varies considerably across architectures. Among the tested models, Gemma 3 shows the strongest English preference while Qwen 3 is the least biased, despite both reaching similar monolingual accuracy across languages. The code is available at https://github.com/ufal/multi-inpaint-coco.

items.title: Steering with Multilingual Lexicons for Sentiment Control in Low-Resource Languages
items.summary: Activation steering offers a lightweight mechanism for controlling model behavior, but existing methods depend on sentence-level contrastive data that is unavailable for most of the world's languages. We show that multilingual sentiment lexicons are a viable substitute across three model families: aggregated multilingual lexicons outperform English-derived steering vectors for mid- and low-resource languages, while monolingual lexicons remain stronger for languages a model has specialized in during pre-training. The steering efficacy is mechanistically dictated by both representational density and pre-training priors. Large-magnitude English vectors overwhelm the compact representations of low-resource languages, causing "linguistic collapse." This fragility is mitigated by the norm-dampening of multilingual aggregation. Architectural biases, including bilingual specialization penalty and latent numerical rigidity, also heavily constrain cross-lingual steering responsiveness. Ultimately, our work establishes lexicons as a practical steering signal and offers a comprehensive mechanistic account of cross-lingual steering dynamics.

items.title: IdeaTaste: Do LLMs Share the Research Taste of Human Researchers?
items.summary: Research taste, the judgment of what to read, which problems to pursue, and which methods to try, increasingly shapes the work of AI scientists, yet it remains far less understood than their ability to execute research. We introduce IdeaTaste, a benchmark that scores an LLM by how closely the research proposals it writes from a literature snapshot frozen at 2025 match the work the same communities published in 2026. Our experiments span six contemporary language models and four research areas from established to emerging fields, covering more than 90{,}000 proposals in total. LLM agents fall well short of human communities in both the literature they cite and the ideas they state, reaching about 26\% of the human level on citation matching and only 18\% on idea matching. Their populations can cite as diversely as a community and take up its tasks and methods, yet rarely arrive at the concrete approaches and research plans it pursues. Neither richer field context nor larger populations substantially close this gap. In blinded expert review, AI proposals trail the 2026 papers least in presentation and most in expected success, echoing their gap in concrete approaches, and those whose ideas no human paper shares fare worst, suggesting weaker directions rather than overlooked opportunities. These results indicate that the main bottleneck in AI research taste lies less in finding the directions a community works on than in turning them into the concrete approaches it goes on to pursue. We release IdeaTaste as an open, continuously updated leaderboard (https://cxcscmu.github.io/IdeaTaste) that benchmarks contemporary AI proposals against future publication cycles.

items.title: VIAS: Value-Isolating Activation Steering for Multi-Value Alignment and Compliance for Organisations
items.summary: Organisations increasingly deploy large language model agents that must follow organisational values. We check whether activation steering, which adds vectors to a model's internal activations during generation without changing its weights, can improve compliance beyond prompting alone. Since most scenarios involve several values at once, we focus on multi-value steering. A simple way to build these vectors is to contrast responses that follow all values relevant to a scenario with responses that violate them. However, this gives nearly identical vectors for different values: they capture a general compliance signal rather than individual values, which limits their use when combining several values. We propose Value-Isolating Activation Steering (VIAS), which contrasts responses to the same scenario under two prompts, one listing all relevant values and one omitting a single target value. We keep a pair only if the target value changes from compliant to non-compliant and both responses still meet a minimum compliance level on the other values. We evaluate VIAS on PROTECT, a workplace compliance dataset where each scenario is tagged with relevant values from a 21-value taxonomy. VIAS reduces overlap between value vectors, making them better suited for multi-value steering, although this alone does not lead to independent control over each value. Combined with prompting, VIAS complies with every tagged value on 69.6% of scenarios for Qwen2.5-7B, 75.2% for Mistral-7B, and 72.6% for Phi-3.5-mini, outperforming prompting alone for all three models.

items.title: Can LLM Agents Be Forward-Deployed Engineers? Requirement Discovery and Delivery for Enterprise Text-to-SQL
items.summary: LLM coding agents can increasingly automate model post-training, but whether they can act as forward-deployed engineer (FDE) agents, discovering customer requirements and turning them into deployment decisions, remains unclear. We study this on a real enterprise text-to-SQL engagement: a simulated customer, grounded in the real use case's requirements, starts with an ambiguous request. An agent must discover acceptance criteria, data permissions, and hardware constraints in the discovery phase, then plan and execute a post-training recipe in the delivery phase. Across 15 models, the strongest discover over 80% of withheld requirements and open-weight models discover 40-50%; in the delivery phase, only 25% of runs across eight coding-agent configurations pass all acceptance criteria. We identify four bottlenecks in this engagement: (1) incomplete discovery, with 40% of withheld requirements missing or misrepresented; (2) unreliable execution; (3) underused compute budgets and a lack of systematic comparisons across base models and post-training methods; and (4) benchmark accuracy does not guarantee production readiness. We suggest human review of discovered requirements, monitoring of the agent's plan during execution, and an explicit experiment-environment specification covering hardware, budget scope, and production checks.

items.title: VeriHarm-Bench: Measuring Harmful Success in LLM Coding Agents Verifiably
items.summary: Large language model (LLM) coding agents increasingly operate with shell access, allowing them to write scripts, move files, alter permissions, and modify system configurations. However, an agent may achieve a user's goal while causing unintended harm, such as deleting unrelated files, weakening access controls, or corrupting data, in response to benign inputs without explicit jailbreaking. This failure mode is particularly important because apparent task success may reassure users that an agent behaved correctly, causing harmful side effects to go unnoticed. We call this harmful success: the agent successfully completes the intended benign task while simultaneously causing unintended harm. Despite its importance, harmful success is difficult to measure because conventional task-success metrics overlook harmful behaviors, while existing safety evaluations are often designed solely to assess harmful outcomes. We introduce VeriHarm, an automatic framework for constructing programmatically verifiable benchmarks that directly measure harmful success. VeriHarm minimally perturbs coding tasks to elicit unintended harmful behavior while maintaining the benignity of the task and preserving the original task objective. It then synthesizes executable harm tests that, together with the original task-correctness tests, evaluate both task accuracy and harmful outcomes. Frontier agents, including GPT-5.6-Sol and Claude-Opus-5, achieve an average task accuracy of 95% on our curated VeriHarm-Bench, yet still struggle to complete tasks safely: their safe success rate, the fraction of tasks completed successfully without triggering the designated harm, averages only 37%. These results suggest that successful task completion can frequently coexist with unintended harm, and that task-success metrics alone may substantially understate the potential safety risks of coding agents.

items.title: NitiBench+: A Temporal Thai Legal Question Answering Benchmark Across 17 Domains
items.summary: Law changes over time. A court decides a case under the law in force on that day, and legal QA benchmarks grade answers against today's law. We checked 156,650 decisions of four Thai courts. Up to 67% of them cite law that has since been amended or repealed. We introduce NitiBench+, the sequel of our NitiBench, a Thai legal QA benchmark with 1,670 items across 17 domains, built from decisions of three courts. For each cited section it holds both the text in force on the decision date and the current text, and its retrieval corpus holds every dated version of every Thai statute section. Answers are graded on the Thai Bar Council rubric, the Bar-standard score, and on the overlap between the cited sections and the court's. The report has two parts. Part I measures the cost of the wrong text on 13 open-weight models. Reading the current text of amended law drops the Bar-standard score by 0.25 and missing repealed law drops it by 0.79. The penalty comes from rule changes, 0.45 on the 428 rule-changed items and none on the 331 wording-only items, and Citation F1 does not see it. The text in force is the fair setting. Part II benchmarks today's models on that setting. A public leaderboard ranks 26 models on a held-out test split of 500 items stratified by domain, with a validation split of the same shape released for public use, from memory alone, with the court's sections provided, and as a retrieval agent over the law in force, with the cost per item and the hallucinated citations. The best model scores 7.78 out of 10 and the best open-weight model 6.39. Without a search tool only five open-weight models recall any Thai law, and with it twenty of the 26 models gain and six lose. Leaderboard will take new models as they are released. Legal benchmarks must track dates, and on the right text today's models still leave a wide gap on Thai law.

items.title: ufakzeka-kulak: Building and Evaluating a 31.6M-Parameter Turkish Speech Recognizer from Scratch
items.summary: ufakzeka-kulak is an open Turkish speech-to-text model of 31.6M parameters, a FastConformer encoder with a token-and-duration transducer (TDT) and a CTC head, trained from scratch and released under Apache-2.0. It writes cased, punctuated Turkish with numbers as words. Its 4,977 training hours come from sources whose licences allow commercial use; 281 hours are human-transcribed, and for the other 4,696 the training text is an uploader subtitle or a machine transcript, kept only where a second, independent reading of the audio agrees with it. The recipe, checkpoint, labelling and export choices were made on development data, and the test sets were scored once, in a release gate fixed before training. With greedy TDT decoding the normalised word error rate (WER) is 0.0921 (95 percent interval 0.0792 to 0.1055) on FLEURS Turkish test and 0.0916 (0.0873 to 0.0958) on Common Voice 27.0 Turkish test, lower than Whisper base and Whisper small on both sets with paired intervals wholly below zero; Whisper large-v3 (greedy) scores 0.0604 and 0.0767. On conversational speech the WER is 0.3807. We also report punctuation and casing, degraded audio, and how closely each shipped export reproduces the trained model.

items.title: Tracing the Scientific Discovery Capacity of LLMs to Their Training Data
items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) show growing promise for scientific discovery, yet basic questions remain about what enables reliable discovery. How can we trace the scientific discovery capacity of LLMs to their training data? We study this question as one of missing probability mass and develop a theoretical account in which monofacts-the facts observed once during training-set the discovery capacity. In materials science and regulatory genomics, we directly manipulate monofact rates in training sets and find that more monofacts consistently yield more discoveries across two open-weight model families, sampling strategies, and reasoning budgets. Further experiments show the relationship cannot be explained by training-set diversity alone and can transfer across scientific domains when paired with in-domain data. Together, our results identify monofact rate in training data as a key factor governing discoveries in language models.

items.summary_html:
Tencent’s WeChat Vision team has released WeVisOne-VL, an open vision language model in 2B and 4B sizes. The WeVisOne-VL vision language model handles detection, referring, counting, pointing, OCR, segmentation and alpha matting in one model. Pixel outputs come from a 9.6M-parameter decoder, so no separate SAM is needed. It also answers “None” when a queried object is absent. For developers, that can replace a detector, an OCR engine and a segmenter with one model.

TL;DR
  • Size: 2B (2.44B params) and 4B (4.83B params) on Hugging Face, and a 9.6M-parameter pixel decoder. Trained with up to 8,192 tokens of context; deployment context length is not disclosed.
  • Runs on: A single GPU through Transformers or vLLM in BF16. The package also lists NPU and CPU devices. VRAM needs are not disclosed. A community GGUF ran object-level tasks on a 6 GB RTX 2060.
  • Performance: Beats the same-scale VLM baselines in Tencent’s tables on most of 30+ benchmarks (self-reported).
  • Best: 71.3 F1 Mean on Dense200 dense detection, versus 58.7 for LocateAnything-3B.
  • Worst: 52.6% rejection rate on PR-Bench, so many absent-target queries still get a box.
What is WeVisOne-VL?

WeVisOne-VL (“WeChat Vision All-in-One”) is a perception-focused model from Tencent built on Qwen3-VL. It targets fine-grained localization rather than open-ended chat. Users choose the output granularity: points, boxes, binary masks or continuous alpha mattes.

How does WeVisOne-VL work?

Every task is cast as structured next-token prediction. The model adds coordinate tokens <0> to <1000> for normalized boxes and points. An absent target produces None instead of a guessed box.

For pixel tasks, the model emits an token after each predicted box. Its hidden state becomes a query for the pixel decoder, according to the model card. The decoder has 3 parts:

  • Visual Feature Adapter: reuses multi-level Qwen3-VL ViT features instead of a second image encoder.
  • Box-Guided Query Decoder: 6 deformable cross-attention blocks seeded by the state and the box.
  • Dense Prediction Head: refines output at S/4, S/2 and S/1 into a full-resolution mask or matte.
How was it trained?

A knowledge-graph-driven data engine annotated over 100M images with about 3.6B boxes. SAM3, Rex-Omni and an in-house detector proposed regions, and Qwen3-VL verified them.

Training used 3 SFT stages. Stage 1 aligned output formats on 90M examples. Stage 2 raised input to 1,960 visual tokens and up to 500 boxes per response. Stage 3 trained the pixel decoder, then specialized it for matting on 130M samples. A final GRPO stage used 178K uncertainty-filtered examples, as described in the research paper.

How does WeVisOne-VL perform on benchmarks?

All numbers below are self-reported, using greedy decoding and at most 1,960 visual tokens per image. Detection, referring and OCR use F1 averaged over IoU 0.5 to 0.95.

  • Detection: 55.3 F1 on LVIS and 71.3 on Dense200 for the 4B model.
  • Referring: 81.8 F1 on RefCOCOg test, versus 77.6 for LocateAnything-3B.
  • Rejection: 96.4% on Tencent’s in-house WeRef-Bench (2,880 queries), versus 73.0%.
  • Counting: 89.6% exact-match on PixMo-Count test, versus 82.8%.
  • OCR: 52.0 F1 on TotalText, ahead of the PP-OCRv5 specialist at 25.7.
  • Segmentation: 71.2 gIoU on ReasonSeg val, versus 65.0 for LISA-13B.
  • Matting: 7.3 MAD on P3M-500-NP box prompts, versus 15.4 for SAM2-Matting (SAM3). Lower is better.

The 2B model trails the 4B model on most tasks. It still scores better box-prompted matting on P3M-500-NP, at 6.6 MAD.

Weights for the 2B and 4B models are on Hugging Face. The wevisone_vl package wraps Transformers and vLLM backends. Tasks include detection, referring, point, count_box, ocr, segmentation and matting.

from wevisone_vl import WeVisOneVL
model = WeVisOneVL("tencent/WeVisOne-VL-4B", backend="transformers")  # or "vllm"
result = model.predict(image, task="matting", query="person")

Hosted demos are live for 2B and 4B. Tencent also open-sourced Mask2Alpha, the matting annotator from its data engine. Fine-tuning code is still on the TODO list. GGUF builds cannot produce masks, since the decoder needs native visual features.

Key Takeaways
  • 1 model covers detection, OCR, counting, pointing, segmentation and matting.
  • A 9.6M-parameter decoder replaces SAM for masks and alpha mattes.
  • 4B scores 71.3 F1 on Dense200, 12.6 points above LocateAnything-3B.
  • Apache 2.0 weights, unlike non-commercial LocateAnything-3B.

items.title: Canva to Lay Off 1,271 Employees, 22% of Workforce to Be Affected
items.summary: Canva will lay off 1,271 employees, 22% of its workforce, as part of an organisational restructuring to prepare the company for its next phase of growth. In a memo to employees on November 4, Co-Founder and CEO Melanie Perkins said the changes would involve restructuring teams, relocating some employees to centralised hubs and changing the roles and skills the company needs. The restructuring will also bring product, growth, and platform teams under a single Product organisation, reduce management layers, and consolidate specialised roles into broader positions. “This has been our hardest year yet, and as we shared earlier this year, our growth has slowed for the first time in a decade,” Perkins said in the memo. Founded in 2013, Canva has grown into a design platform used by hundreds of millions of people worldwide. Perkins said the company needs to return to its founding approach of smaller, empowered teams as it prepares for the next decade. She added that the company had explored several alternatives before concluding that smaller changes would not be enough to prepare it for the next decade. As part of the restructuring, Sydney will become the primary location for more of Canva’s product teams and certain other specialist roles. The company said it would continue investing in its global workforce but wants teams working on closely connected areas to collaborate more frequently in person. From January, most employees working under its hybrid model are expected to spend two to three days a week in the office, depending on their location. Canva also plans to reduce the number of specialised teams and simplify reporting structures to give employees greater ownership of projects. “We want to get back to spending more time building, and less time navigating how work gets done,” Perkins said. Canva said employees leaving the company will receive at least six months’ salary, including statutory entitlements, regardless of their location. The support package also includes 12 months of healthcare coverage in countries where the company currently provides it, along with continued access to its employee assistance programme for employees and their families. Employees who joined within the past year will also have their one-year vesting cliff removed. The company will provide career support, including individual coaching, interview preparation and one year of LinkedIn Premium. Departing employees will also be allowed to keep their company-issued MacBooks. Canva is also launching the Canva Collective Fund, which will provide $10,000 grants to departing employees interested in starting a business or pursuing community projects. The company said it would not take equity or ownership in the ventures.

items.title: Journify Raises $12M Series A Amid 5x Growth
items.summary: Investors back Journify’s push into the US and Europe Journify , the ad signal infrastructure company, today announced a $12 million Series A at four times its previous valuation. Al Mada Ventures led the round, co-led by returning investor Silicon Badia, with Shorooq and Bunat Ventures increasing their investment and Du Ventures and Oraseya Capital joining as new investors. The funding will take Journify into the US and Europe and expand the AI behind its platform. Global ad spend will exceed $1 trillion in 2026, with algorithms expected to place three quarters by 2028, according to dentsu. These systems learn from the customer outcomes brands send back. Browser restrictions, broken tracking, and disconnected offline sales leave them with an incomplete picture of who buys. Journify makes sure ad platforms such as Google, Meta, TikTok, Snap and Amazon Ads see the purchases, sign-ups and store sales a brand’s customers actually make. More than 100 businesses use Journify today, from fast-growing ecommerce brands to some of the region’s largest retailers, representing hundreds of millions of dollars in annual ad spend. Customers include Jarir Bookstore, one of Saudi Arabia’s largest retailers, which increased its return on ad spend on Meta by 182%, and Saudi ecommerce brand Baytonia, which grew its return on ad spend on TikTok by 80% while cutting cost per purchase by 44%. “AI is transforming advertising, but the intelligence behind it is only as good as the signals it receives,” said Taoufik El Jamali, Co-Founder and CEO of Journify. “Businesses know who buys, who comes back and what creates lasting customer value. Too little of that knowledge reaches the ad platforms driving their growth. Our vision is to close that gap, turning real customer outcomes into intelligence ad platforms can learn from. We’re building toward a future where advertising AI understands what makes a customer valuable to each business, not just what makes them click.”“As AI takes on a greater role in marketing, we believe the connection between reliable customer data and the decisions built on it will become increasingly valuable,” said Omar Laalej, Managing Director at Al Mada Ventures. “What interests us about Journify is its approach to building that connection from the data layer up: a privacy-first foundation that can evolve into intelligence and action. The founders’ understanding of that opportunity gives us confidence in their ability to build a platform that marketers can increasingly rely on, both to understand their customers and to act on that understanding.”Hossam Shafick, Partner at Silicon Badia, Seed Lead and returning investor, added, “Since our initial investment, Journify has grown its valuation by more than 4x, and its revenues more than 5x, validating both the strength of its technology and the team’s ability to execute at scale. That performance has deepened our conviction that Journify can become a global leader in ad signal infrastructure. We are proud to double down and co-lead this round as the company expands into the world’s largest advertising markets.” Journify already uses AI to monitor every connection continuously, detect signal-quality issues and fix them. The new funding will grow those capabilities as Journify expands beyond the GCC. In the US alone, digital advertising revenue reached $294.6 billion in 2025, according to IAB and PwC. “I’m excited to help Journify scale in the biggest ad market in the world,” said Ryan Burke, a newly appointed member of Journify’s board and three-time Chief Revenue Officer. “I’ve known Taoufik since our InVision days, and I’ve seen his product execution in action. Based on the success they’re already seeing in the Middle East, it’s not a question whether it works in the US, but how fast we can scale.” About Journify Journify builds ad signal infrastructure for performance marketers. Its privacy-first, real-time data layer helps brands improve the quality and reliability of the first-party signals used in advertising and measurement. Journify connects data across web, mobile, offline sales, CRM, ecommerce platforms, backend systems and data warehouses. It validates and enriches conversion events and activates consented signals server-side across Google, Meta, TikTok, Snap, Amazon Ads and other platforms. Founded in 2022 by Taoufik El Jamali, Amine Chouki and Omar Al Shoubaki, Journify is headquartered in San Francisco with offices in Dubai and Riyadh. Learn more at journify.io . Journify has obtained a SOC 2 Type II report and is committed to GDPR compliance. Contact Head of Marketing Vanessa Moreno Journify vanessa.moreno@journify.io

items.title: IndiaAI Mission Releases 3 Indigenous AI Models Developed by Soket, ZenteiQ
items.summary: The IndiaAI Mission has released three indigenous foundation models: EKA-1 by Soket AI Labs and Dhīr 2B and Dhīr 5B by ZenteiQ AiTech Innovations. EKA-1 is a 26.3-billion-parameter model trained on approximately 7.5 trillion tokens. It supports all 22 scheduled Indian languages and English, with capabilities in mathematics, coding, reasoning and agentic applications. Meanwhile, ZenteiQ’s Dhīr models are open-source multilingual assistants built for on-premise and offline deployment across government, defence, industrial and educational sectors. The models were unveiled at an event in New Delhi on November 3 in the presence of S Krishnan, Secretary at the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY), and senior officials from MeitY and IndiaAI. Soket AI Labs developed EKA-1 as an open, sparse hybrid language model. The company said the model was tailored to India's banking, financial services and cybersecurity sectors. “With the support of the IndiaAI Mission, we have developed an advanced AI model specifically tailored to India's unique banking, financial services and cybersecurity landscape. It is designed to address sector-specific requirements, understand India's evolving digital ecosystem, and deliver solutions aligned with the country's needs and priorities,” said Abhishek Upperwal, CEO of Soket AI Labs. ZenteiQ, meanwhile, introduced Dhīr 2B and Dhīr 5B as open-source models supporting English and 10 Indian languages. The models are built for document-based automation, information retrieval and citizen and enterprise services. They can be deployed on-premise and operate without continuous cloud connectivity. The company said the models could run across different computing platforms, including GPUs and TPUs, with their lightweight architecture also supporting deployment on mobile devices. “Models like Dhīr 2B and Dhīr 5B offer the flexibility to run across different computing platforms, including GPUs and TPUs. Their lightweight architecture also enables on-device deployment on mobile phones, without dependence on cloud connectivity,” said Prof Sashikumar, CEO of ZenteiQ AiTech Innovations. “This allows users to access AI capabilities locally while keeping data on their devices, enhancing privacy, security and accessibility,” he added. The models were developed by teams selected under the IndiaAI Innovation Centre’s Foundation Models pillar. S Krishnan said the development of indigenous models would strengthen India's technological autonomy in artificial intelligence and create opportunities to improve productivity across government, industry, research and education. He also highlighted AIKosh, the IndiaAI platform through which the models can be made available to researchers, students and developers for further experimentation. Sudeep Shrivastava, COO of IndiaAI, said the models reflect progress across different categories of AI development, from lightweight systems for everyday devices to models built for complex enterprise applications.

The IndiaAI Mission has released three indigenous foundation models: EKA-1 by Soket AI Labs and Dhīr 2B and Dhīr 5B by ZenteiQ AiTech Innovations.

EKA-1 is a 26.3-billion-parameter model trained on approximately 7.5 trillion tokens. It supports all 22 scheduled Indian languages and English, with capabilities in mathematics, coding, reasoning and agentic applications. 

Meanwhile, ZenteiQ’s Dhīr models are open-source multilingual assistants built for on-premise and offline deployment across government, defence, industrial and educational sectors.

The models were unveiled at an event in New Delhi on November 3 in the presence of S Krishnan, Secretary at the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY), and senior officials from MeitY and IndiaAI.

Soket AI Labs developed EKA-1 as an open, sparse hybrid language model. The company said the model was tailored to India's banking, financial services and cybersecurity sectors.

“With the support of the IndiaAI Mission, we have developed an advanced AI model specifically tailored to India's unique banking, financial services and cybersecurity landscape. It is designed to address sector-specific requirements, understand India's evolving digital ecosystem, and deliver solutions aligned with the country's needs and priorities,” said Abhishek Upperwal, CEO of Soket AI Labs.

ZenteiQ, meanwhile, introduced Dhīr 2B and Dhīr 5B as open-source models supporting English and 10 Indian languages. The models are built for document-based automation, information retrieval and citizen and enterprise services. They can be deployed on-premise and operate without continuous cloud connectivity.

The company said the models could run across different computing platforms, including GPUs and TPUs, with their lightweight architecture also supporting deployment on mobile devices.

“Models like Dhīr 2B and Dhīr 5B offer the flexibility to run across different computing platforms, including GPUs and TPUs. “This allows users to access AI capabilities locally while keeping data on their devices, enhancing privacy, security and accessibility,” he added.

The models were developed by teams selected under the IndiaAI Innovation Centre’s Foundation Models pillar. The IndiaAI Mission provided access to subsidised national AI compute infrastructure and support for research expenses.

S Krishnan said the development of indigenous models would strengthen India's technological autonomy in artificial intelligence and create opportunities to improve productivity across government, industry, research and education.

He also highlighted AIKosh, the IndiaAI platform through which the models can be made available to researchers, students and developers for further experimentation.

items.title: Anthropic’s $17 Billion Quarter Ended in an Operating Loss: What the IPO Filing Reveals About Compute
items.summary: Anthropic, the developer of Claude, reported $17.0 billion in third-quarter revenue and an operating loss of $567 million, after an operating profit of $974 million in the second quarter. Its amended IPO filing with the US Securities and Exchange Commission, submitted on Nov. 2, attributes the loss primarily to $5.0 billion of compute bought on short-term commitments and $2.0 billion of non-cash charges tied to its donation-matching program. The filing says the short-term capacity costs significantly more than comparable multi-year compute, and it does not say how much more. What the Amended Filing Shows Revenue reached $16.96 billion, up 46.7% from $11.56 billion in the second quarter and 1,127% from a year earlier. Quarterly growth slowed from 144% in the second quarter. Operating expenses rose to $17.5 billion from $10.6 billion, and compute and infrastructure costs climbed to $9.86 billion, or 58% of revenue, from 48% in the second quarter. Adjusted operating income, which excludes stock-based compensation and non-cash charitable charges, rose to $2.5 billion from $2.2 billion. Adjusted operating margin still fell to 15% from 19%, and the filing attributes that decline primarily to the short-term compute. The $23.3 billion net loss sits almost entirely below the operating line, and CNBC reported that changes in the fair value of convertible notes drove most of Anthropic’s $104 billion nine-month net loss. Why Short-Term Compute Costs More Anthropic says it typically procures compute 12 to 18 months before it becomes available. When demand from customers or researchers runs ahead of what those contracts deliver, it buys short-term capacity. The filing says efficiency improvements in the quarter were partially offset by the delivery of additional compute, including $5.0 billion under short-term commitments that “currently costs significantly more than comparable compute procured under our multi-year commitments.” The $5.0 billion is the total spent on that capacity, not the premium over long-term rates, which the filing does not disclose. Management expects the pressure to continue. The filing says Anthropic expects “our use of short-term compute to continue to increase in the near term and to in turn compress our operating margin and Adjusted Operating Margin.” It calls the cycle, in which compute arrives before the revenue it supports, “an inherent aspect of our business.” Enterprise IT teams know the trade from their cloud bills: reserved capacity costs less per unit than on-demand, and the buyer pays for it whether or not demand arrives. The planned fix is a hybrid sourcing model the filing calls Anthropic Direct, which adds leased chips hosted in dedicated facilities operated on Anthropic’s behalf to its fixed-term cloud agreements. Anthropic says the flexibility lets it replace short-term compute bought during periods of high demand with more cost-effective long-term compute as that dedicated infrastructure comes online. What the $895.4 Billion Commitment Total Shows The filing puts Anthropic’s aggregate committed spend on purchase commitments and leases at approximately $895.4 billion, substantially all of it for compute and infrastructure. Roughly $447.5 billion falls due through 2030, including about $69.8 billion in the 12 months after Sept. 30. The filing says a significant portion of the total relates to Anthropic Direct, and that it expects Anthropic Direct to become a growing share of its compute investments. Annualizing third-quarter revenue gives roughly $68 billion, so the next 12 months of commitments roughly match a year of current revenue, and the full total is about 13 times that run rate. Two qualifications cut in opposite directions. About $213.8 billion of the total relates to arrangements subject to exercisable termination rights or contingent conditions, such as a counterparty securing financing, facilities or regulatory approvals. Separately, the total leaves out agreements with no fixed dollar commitment, which Anthropic estimates at approximately $150 billion to $175 billion. Cash is the cushion. Anthropic held about $131.8 billion in cash and short-term investments at Sept. 30, and the filing says it intends to fund these investments “through the revenue we generate and the capital that we raise.” It also says the build-out will be “a significant use of net cash in operating and investing activities for the foreseeable future.” Customer revenue is mostly usage-based: consumption fees made up 79% of nine-month revenue, and remaining performance obligations, the contracted revenue not yet recognized, were $13.8 billion. Price Cuts and Supplier Financing The filing also quantifies what price reductions cost. Between the second and third quarters, higher usage was partly offset by a decrease of approximately $600 million from price reductions introduced with new model versions and contractual discounts, against about $70 million between the third and fourth quarters of 2025. The $600 million equals about 3.5% of third-quarter revenue. The implication for buyers is that a supplier paying more for short-term capacity while cutting prices on new models may have less room to keep cutting. The filing adds a new risk factor: some of Anthropic’s compute partners depend on third-party financing or credit support, and if that financing tightens, contracted capacity “may be delayed, repriced, reduced, or not delivered.” The commitments show where that applies. Under the largest Lambda agreement, either party may terminate if Lambda does not timely secure a facility lease. Anthropic is not alone in the squeeze: Microsoft’s CFO told investors last week that customer demand continues to exceed available supply, and Alphabet said it started using third-party compute capacity at the end of the third quarter. The filing leaves the price range, share count and run-rate revenue as of Oct. 31 blank, so what investors will pay is still open. The fourth quarter will show whether short-term compute shrinks as dedicated capacity comes online, as Anthropic’s plan intends, or grows, as management expects in the near term.
